subproblem.title: Conical density lemma for purely unrectifiable sets (Mattila 15.13-15.15)
subproblem.statement: Let N, m ∈ ℕ and k := m + 1. Let E ⊆ ℝ^N be purely k-unrectifiable (every countably k-rectifiable subset of E has Hᵏ-measure 0, Hᵏ = μHE[k]), let v = (v₁, …, v_k) ∈ (ℝ^N)^k, let L_v : ℝ^N → ℝᵏ be the linear map L_v(x) = (⟨v₁,x⟩, …, ⟨v_k,x⟩), and let δ > 0. For a ∈ ℝ^N and r, s > 0 let X_v(a,r,s) := {x ∈ ℝ^N : |x − a| < r, |L_v(x − a)| < s|x − a|} (the truncated cone of aperture s around the fibre a + ker L_v). Let E₁ be the set of a ∈ E such that for every η > 0 there is s ∈ (0,1) with Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(a,r,s)) ≤ η(rs)ᵏ for all r ∈ (0,δ). Then Hᵏ(E₁) = 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N m : ℕ) (E : Set (Eucl N)) (v : Fin (m + 1) → Eucl N) (δ : ℝ), Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter03.PurelyUnrectifiable (m + 1) E → 0 < δ → (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl N)) {a | a ∈ E ∧ ∀ η : ℝ, 0 < η → ∃ s ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1, ∀ r ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) δ, (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl N)) (E ∩ {x | dist x a < r ∧ ‖(WithLp.toLp 2 (fun i : Fin (m + 1) => inner ℝ (v i) (x - a)) : Eucl (m + 1))‖ < s * ‖x - a‖}) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal (η * (r * s) ^ (m + 1))} = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: P. Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces (Cambridge Univ. Press, 1995): Lemma 15.13 (a cone condition gives a Lipschitz graph), Lemma 15.14 (the conical density estimate) and Corollary 15.15. The statement is the form used by R. Hovila, E. Järvenpää, M. Järvenpää and F. Ledrappier, Besicovitch-Federer projection theorem and geodesic flows on Riemann surfaces, Geom. Dedicata 161 (2012), arXiv:1104.3453, Lemma 2.2 ('E_{1,δ}(λ) has measure zero'). Here the orthogonal projection Q_V is replaced by the linear map L_v; the proof uses only the linearity of L_v and its operator norm ‖L_v‖. Simon's book does not contain this lemma: it belongs to the proof of the Structure Theorem 3.6 of Ch. 3, which Simon cites without proof. The argument is therefore written out in full. Step 1 is the conical density estimate; its 'graph part' is the Lipschitz-graph criterion. Step 2 is the covering argument behind the lower bound for upper densities of Hausdorff measure (Mattila 6.2(1); Simon Ch. 1, 3.26(2)), in the uniform form needed here. Step 3 combines them.

Notation: k := m + 1 and Hᵏ := μHE[k], an outer measure on ℝ^N. All inequalities below are for outer measures, so no measurability is needed. B(x,ρ) and B̄(x,ρ) are the open and closed balls, ω_k := Lᵏ(B(0,1)), and Z(a,ρ) := {x : |L_v(x − a)| < ρ} = L_v^{-1}(B(L_va,ρ)) is the cylinder around the fibre a + ker L_v. Note that X_v(a,r,s) ⊆ X_v(a,r,s′) for s ≤ s′, and that a ∉ X_v(a,r,s).

1. Conical density estimate (Mattila 15.14). Claim: let B ⊆ E, s ∈ (0,1), δ′ > 0 and λ ≥ 0 satisfy Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(a,r,s)) ≤ λ(rs)ᵏ for all a ∈ B and 0 < r ≤ δ′. Then Hᵏ(B ∩ B(x₀,δ′/6)) ≤ C₁λδ′ᵏ for every x₀ ∈ ℝ^N, where C₁ := 2(20/3)ᵏ(‖L_v‖ + 1)ᵏ.
 Proof. Let F := B ∩ B(x₀,δ′/6), so diam F ≤ δ′/3. Write X_v(a,∞,s/4) := {x : |L_v(x − a)| < (s/4)|x − a|}. For a ∈ F let h(a) := sup{|b − a| : b ∈ F ∩ X_v(a,∞,s/4)}, with sup ∅ := 0, so 0 ≤ h(a) ≤ δ′/3. Let F₀ := {a ∈ F : h(a) = 0} and F₁ := F∖F₀.
 (a) The graph part (Mattila 15.13). Let a, b ∈ F₀ be distinct. Then b ∉ X_v(a,∞,s/4), since otherwise h(a) ≥ |b − a| > 0; that is, |L_v(b − a)| ≥ (s/4)|b − a|. Hence L_v is injective on F₀, and g := (L_v|F₀)^{-1} : L_v(F₀) → ℝ^N is (4/s)-Lipschitz. Extend each of the N coordinates of g to a (4/s)-Lipschitz function on ℝᵏ (McShane; Mathlib LipschitzOnWith.extend_real). This gives a Lipschitz map G : ℝᵏ → ℝ^N with F₀ = g(L_v(F₀)) ⊆ G(ℝᵏ). By Simon Ch. 3, 1.1 (SimonGMT countablyRectifiable_range, CountablyRectifiable.mono), F₀ is countably k-rectifiable. Since F₀ ⊆ E and E is purely k-unrectifiable, Hᵏ(F₀) = 0.
 (b) Two cones cover a cylinder. Let a ∈ F₁ and h := h(a) > 0. By the definition of the supremum choose b = b(a) ∈ F ∩ X_v(a,∞,s/4) with |b − a| > 3h/4; also |b − a| ≤ h. Put ρ(a) := sh/20.
 We claim F ∩ Z(a,5ρ(a)) ⊆ X_v(a,2h,s) ∪ X_v(b,2h,s). Let c ∈ F with |L_v(c − a)| < 5ρ(a) = sh/4.
 First, |c − a| ≤ h. Otherwise |L_v(c − a)| < sh/4 < (s/4)|c − a|, so c ∈ F ∩ X_v(a,∞,s/4) and hence |c − a| ≤ h(a) = h, a contradiction.
 If |c − a| ≥ h/4, then |L_v(c − a)| < sh/4 ≤ s|c − a| and |c − a| ≤ h < 2h, so c ∈ X_v(a,2h,s).
 If |c − a| < h/4, then |c − b| ≥ |b − a| − |c − a| > 3h/4 − h/4 = h/2 and |c − b| ≤ |c − a| + |a − b| < h/4 + h < 2h. Also |L_v(c − b)| ≤ |L_v(c − a)| + |L_v(a − b)| < sh/4 + (s/4)|a − b| ≤ sh/2 < s|c − b|. So c ∈ X_v(b,2h,s).
 Since a, b ∈ F ⊆ B and 2h ≤ 2δ′/3 ≤ δ′, the hypothesis gives
 Hᵏ(F ∩ Z(a,5ρ(a))) ≤ Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(a,2h,s)) + Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(b,2h,s)) ≤ 2λ(2hs)ᵏ = 2λ(40ρ(a))ᵏ.
 (c) Covering. The open balls B(L_va,ρ(a)) ⊆ ℝᵏ (a ∈ F₁) have radii ≤ sδ′/60. Apply the Vitali covering lemma (Mathlib Vitali.exists_disjoint_subfamily_covering_enlargement with enlargement factor τ = 2). It gives a pairwise disjoint subfamily {B(L_va_i,ρ_i)} (ρ_i := ρ(a_i)) such that every ball B(L_va,ρ(a)) of the family meets some B(L_va_i,ρ_i) with ρ(a) ≤ 2ρ_i, hence B(L_va,ρ(a)) ⊆ B(L_va_i,5ρ_i). The subfamily is countable, since disjoint nonempty open sets in ℝᵏ are countably many. Consequently F₁ ⊆ ⋃_{a∈F₁}Z(a,ρ(a)) ⊆ ⋃_iZ(a_i,5ρ_i).
 Since |L_va_i − L_vx₀| ≤ ‖L_v‖|a_i − x₀| ≤ ‖L_v‖δ′/6 and ρ_i ≤ sδ′/60 < δ′/6, each B(L_va_i,ρ_i) lies in B(L_vx₀,(‖L_v‖ + 1)δ′/6). By disjointness, Σ_iω_kρ_iᵏ ≤ ω_k((‖L_v‖ + 1)δ′/6)ᵏ.
 (d) Conclusion. By countable subadditivity and (a)-(c), Hᵏ(F) ≤ Hᵏ(F₀) + Σ_iHᵏ(F ∩ Z(a_i,5ρ_i)) ≤ 2λ40ᵏΣ_iρ_iᵏ ≤ 2λ40ᵏ((‖L_v‖ + 1)/6)ᵏδ′ᵏ = C₁λδ′ᵏ. ∎

2. Uniform density bounds force measure zero (Mattila 6.2(1)). By the definition of euclideanHausdorffMeasure, Hᵏ = c_k·μH[k] with a constant c_k ∈ (0,∞): μHE[k] = volume.addHaarScalarFactor μH[k] • μH[k]. Here μH[k](S) = sup_{ε>0}inf{Σ_j(diam C_j)ᵏ : S ⊆ ⋃_jC_j, diam C_j ≤ ε}, where only nonempty C_j count (Mathlib hausdorffMeasure_apply).
 Claim: suppose B ⊆ ℝ^N, ρ₀ > 0 and 0 ≤ c₀ < c_k satisfy Hᵏ(B ∩ B̄(x,ρ)) ≤ c₀ρᵏ for all x ∈ B and 0 < ρ ≤ ρ₀. Then Hᵏ(B) = 0.
 Proof. Fix x₁ ∈ B and let B′ := B ∩ B(x₁,ρ₀/2). Then Hᵏ(B′) ≤ Hᵏ(B ∩ B̄(x₁,ρ₀/2)) ≤ c₀(ρ₀/2)ᵏ < ∞, and B′ satisfies the same hypothesis.
 Let 0 < ε ≤ ρ₀ and let (C_j) be a countable cover of B′ by sets of diameter ≤ ε, each meeting B′ (discard the others). Pick x_j ∈ C_j ∩ B′ and put d_j := diam C_j ≤ ρ₀. If d_j > 0, then C_j ⊆ B̄(x_j,d_j), so Hᵏ(B′ ∩ C_j) ≤ c₀d_jᵏ. If d_j = 0, then B′ ∩ C_j = {x_j} and Hᵏ({x_j}) = 0 because k ≥ 1. Hence Hᵏ(B′) ≤ Σ_jHᵏ(B′ ∩ C_j) ≤ c₀Σ_jd_jᵏ.
 Taking the infimum over such covers and letting ε ↓ 0 gives Hᵏ(B′) ≤ c₀μH[k](B′) = (c₀/c_k)Hᵏ(B′). Since Hᵏ(B′) < ∞ and c₀ < c_k, Hᵏ(B′) = 0. Finally, B is covered by countably many balls B(x₁,ρ₀/2) with x₁ in a countable dense subset of B, so Hᵏ(B) = 0. ∎

3. Proof of the statement. Put η₀ := c_k/(2C₁·24ᵏ) > 0. For a rational s′ ∈ (0,1) let B_{s′} := {a ∈ E : Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(a,r,s′)) ≤ 2ᵏη₀(rs′)ᵏ for all r ∈ (0,δ)}.
 (a) E₁ ⊆ ⋃_{s′∈ℚ∩(0,1)}B_{s′}. Let a ∈ E₁. Take η := η₀ and the corresponding s ∈ (0,1), and choose a rational s′ ∈ (s/2,s). For r ∈ (0,δ), X_v(a,r,s′) ⊆ X_v(a,r,s), so Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(a,r,s′)) ≤ η₀(rs)ᵏ ≤ 2ᵏη₀(rs′)ᵏ. Thus a ∈ B_{s′}.
 (b) Hᵏ(B_{s′}) = 0. Let x ∈ B_{s′} and 0 < ρ < δ/12. Apply step 1 with B := B_{s′} ⊆ E, s := s′, λ := 2ᵏη₀, δ′ := 12ρ < δ and x₀ := x; its hypothesis holds because 0 < r ≤ δ′ < δ. This gives Hᵏ(B_{s′} ∩ B̄(x,ρ)) ≤ Hᵏ(B_{s′} ∩ B(x,δ′/6)) ≤ C₁2ᵏη₀(12ρ)ᵏ = (c_k/2)ρᵏ, using B̄(x,ρ) ⊆ B(x,2ρ) = B(x,δ′/6). Step 2 with c₀ := c_k/2 and ρ₀ := δ/13 then gives Hᵏ(B_{s′}) = 0.
 Hence Hᵏ(E₁) ≤ Σ_{s′}Hᵏ(B_{s′}) = 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: Lipschitz-graph criterion (Mattila 15.13): let F₀ be the points of F whose s/4-cone contains no other point of F. L_v is injective on F₀ with Lipschitz inverse, so F₀ is a countably k-rectifiable, hence Hᵏ-null, subset of E.
Two-cone covering: for every other point a, the part of F in the cylinder Z(a,5ρ(a)) lies in X_v(a,2h,s) ∪ X_v(b(a),2h,s), so its measure is at most 2λ(40ρ(a))ᵏ.
Vitali covering of the projected balls B(L_va,ρ(a)) in ℝᵏ gives Σρ_iᵏ ≤ ((‖L_v‖+1)δ′/6)ᵏ, hence Hᵏ(B ∩ B(x₀,δ′/6)) ≤ C₁λδ′ᵏ (Mattila 15.14).
A uniform bound Hᵏ(B ∩ B̄(x,ρ)) ≤ c₀ρᵏ with c₀ below the Hausdorff normalization constant forces Hᵏ(B) = 0 (covering definition of Hᵏ).
E₁ lies in countably many sets B_{s′} (s′ rational) with small cone ratios; the two previous steps make each B_{s′} null.

audit.reason: The Lipschitz inverse handles the graph part; the two-cone inclusion and disjoint projected balls give the stated uniform bound. The Hausdorff-cover argument and rational-aperture reduction then prove the exact quantified conclusion without assuming E measurable or finite. This is consistent with [Hovila et al., §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1104.3453).

subproblem.title: Comparison of upper density with Hausdorff measure (Simon 1, Theorem 3.3)
subproblem.statement: For all P, n ∈ ℕ, every Borel measure ν on ℝ^P, every open V ⊆ ℝ^P, every set A ⊆ V (not necessarily measurable) and every t ∈ [0, ∞]: if the upper density Θ*ⁿ(ν, x) := limsup_{r↓0} ν(B̄_r(x))/(ω_n rⁿ) (dimensionalUpperDensity ν n univ x) satisfies Θ*ⁿ(ν, x) ≥ t for every x ∈ A, then t·Hⁿ(A) ≤ ν(V), where Hⁿ(A) = μHE[n](A) is the outer n-dimensional Hausdorff measure.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (ν : Measure (Eucl P)) (A V : Set (Eucl P)) (t : ℝ≥0∞), IsOpen V → A ⊆ V → (∀ x ∈ A, t ≤ dimensionalUpperDensity ν.toOuterMeasure (n : ℝ) univ x) → t * (μHE[n] : Measure (Eucl P)) A ≤ ν V
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 1, Theorem 3.3 and its printed proof (p. 15) with A₁ := A and A₂ := V, using the 5-times covering lemma 3.4 and Corollary 3.5. (SimonGMT formalizes exactly this argument: mul_simonHausdorff_le_of_le_dimensionalUpperDensity, together with dimensionalUpperDensity_inter_of_mem_nhds and simonHausdorffMeasureReal_nat_eq_euclideanHausdorffMeasure.)

1. Normalizations. The outer measure of ν (ν(S) = inf{ν(B) : B ⊇ S Borel}) is Borel regular and all Borel sets are ν-measurable (Carathéodory), as required in 3.3. Simon's Hausdorff measure Hⁿ (covers by sets C of diameter < δ with cost ω_n (diam C/2)ⁿ, then δ ↓ 0) coincides with μHE[n] as an outer measure on ℝ^P: both are the n-dimensional Hausdorff measure normalized to agree with Lⁿ on ℝⁿ (Simon Ch. 1, 2.8-2.10; SimonGMT simonHausdorffMeasureReal_nat_eq_euclideanHausdorffMeasure and simonHausdorffMeasureReal_toOuterMeasure). Write Θ*ⁿ(ν, V, x) := limsup_{r↓0} ν(V ∩ B̄_r(x))/(ω_n rⁿ) (Simon (3.1)).

2. Localization. If x ∈ A ⊆ V and V is open, there is R > 0 with B̄_R(x) ⊆ V, so ν(V ∩ B̄_r(x)) = ν(B̄_r(x)) for 0 < r < R and Θ*ⁿ(ν, V, x) = Θ*ⁿ(ν, x) ≥ t. So the hypothesis of 3.3 holds with A₁ = A ⊆ A₂ = V.

3. Trivial cases. If t = 0 or ν(V) = ∞ there is nothing to prove. If t = ∞, then the hypothesis holds with every real t′ > 0 in place of t, so by the case 0 < t′ < ∞ below t′ Hⁿ(A) ≤ ν(V) for all such t′; hence either Hⁿ(A) = 0 (and ∞·0 = 0 ≤ ν(V)) or ν(V) = ∞. So assume 0 < t < ∞ and ν(V) < ∞.

4. Printed proof of 3.3. Take τ ∈ (0, t), so Θ*ⁿ(ν, V, x) > τ for every x ∈ A. For δ > 0 let 𝓑 be the family of closed balls B̄_ρ(x) with x ∈ A, 0 < ρ < δ/2 and ν(V ∩ B̄_ρ(x)) ≥ τ ω_n ρⁿ. By the definition of the limsup, 𝓑 covers A finely. By the 5-times covering lemma 3.4 there is a pairwise disjoint subfamily 𝓑′ ⊆ 𝓑 such that every B ∈ 𝓑 meets some B′ ∈ 𝓑′ with diam B′ ≥ diam B/2, hence B is contained in the concentric ball B̂′ with 5 times the radius of B′. Since ν(V ∩ B) > 0 for B ∈ 𝓑 and, for finitely many disjoint B_1, …, B_N ∈ 𝓑′, Σ_j ν(V ∩ B_j) = ν(V ∩ ⋃_j B_j) ≤ ν(V) < ∞, the family 𝓑′ is countable, 𝓑′ = {B̄_{ρ_j}(x_j) : j ≥ 1}, and Σ_j ω_n ρ_jⁿ ≤ τ^{-1} Σ_j ν(V ∩ B̄_{ρ_j}(x_j)) ≤ τ^{-1} ν(V) < ∞. By Corollary 3.5, A ∖ ⋃_{j ≤ N} B̄_{ρ_j}(x_j) ⊆ ⋃_{j > N} B̄_{5ρ_j}(x_j) for every N. These balls have diameter < 5δ and a ball of radius ρ has cost ω_n (diam/2)ⁿ ≤ ω_n ρⁿ, so by the definition of Hⁿ_{5δ}: Hⁿ_{5δ}(A) ≤ Σ_{j ≤ N} ω_n ρ_jⁿ + 5ⁿ Σ_{j > N} ω_n ρ_jⁿ. Letting N → ∞ (the tail of a convergent series tends to 0) gives Hⁿ_{5δ}(A) ≤ Σ_j ω_n ρ_jⁿ ≤ τ^{-1} ν(V).

5. Letting δ ↓ 0 gives τ Hⁿ(A) ≤ ν(V), and letting τ ↑ t gives t Hⁿ(A) ≤ ν(V). By step 1 this is t·μHE[n](A) ≤ ν(V). (For n = 0 the same argument applies with ω_0 = 1 and ρ⁰ = 1.) ∎
proof_key_steps: Identify Simon's Hⁿ with μHE[n] (outer measures) and use Borel regularity of ν.
For x ∈ A ⊆ V with V open, Θ*ⁿ(ν, V, x) = Θ*ⁿ(ν, x) ≥ t, so Theorem 3.3 applies with A₁ = A, A₂ = V.
Dispose of t ∈ {0, ∞} and ν(V) = ∞.
Fine cover of A by balls with ν(V ∩ B̄_ρ(x)) ≥ τω_nρⁿ; the 5-times covering lemma gives a countable disjoint subfamily with Σ ω_nρ_jⁿ ≤ τ⁻¹ν(V).
Corollary 3.5 bounds Hⁿ_{5δ}(A) by the subfamily's cost; let δ ↓ 0 and τ ↑ t.

subproblem.title: Riesz representation of a locally finite mass current with respect to its mass measure (Simon 6, (2.7)-(2.8))
subproblem.statement: Let P, k ∈ ℕ, let U ⊆ ℝ^P be open and let T ∈ D_k(U) (GeometricCurrentOn U k) satisfy M_W(T) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U. Then (i) there is a Borel measure μ on ℝ^P with IsMassMeasure T μ, i.e. μ(ℝ^P∖U) = 0 and μ(W) = M_W(T) for every open W ⊂⊂ U; and (ii) for every Borel measure μ on ℝ^P with IsMassMeasure T μ there is a strongly measurable k-vector field ξ : ℝ^P → Λ_k(ℝ^P) (NVector) of Euclidean coefficient norm 1 μ-a.e., i.e. Σ_{α ∈ I(k,P)} ξ(x)(dx^α)² = 1 for μ-a.e. x (dx^α = dx^{α(1)}∧⋯∧dx^{α(k)}, euclideanNVectorCoordinate), such that for every ω ∈ D^k(U) the function x ↦ ⟨ω(x), ξ(x)⟩ = ξ(x)(ω(x)) is μ-integrable and T(ω) = ∫⟨ω(x), ξ(x)⟩ dμ(x) (IsMeasureRepresentation T μ ξ).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P k : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)), IsOpen U → ∀ T : GeometricCurrentOn U k, (∀ W, CompactlyContainedOpen W U → T.massOn W < ∞) → (∃ μ : Measure (Eucl P), IsMassMeasure T μ) ∧ ∀ μ : Measure (Eucl P), IsMassMeasure T μ → ∃ ξ : Eucl P → NVector (Eucl P) k, StronglyMeasurable ξ ∧ (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, ∑ α : SimonMultiIndex k P, (euclideanNVectorCoordinate (ξ x) α) ^ 2 = 1) ∧ IsMeasureRepresentation T μ ξ
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, (2.7)-(2.8) (p. 136): ‘by the Riesz Representation Theorem 4.14 of Ch. 1 we have that if T ∈ D_n(U) satisfies M_W(T) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U, then there is a Radon measure μ_T on U and μ_T-measurable T⃗ with values in Λ_n(ℝ^P), |T⃗| = 1 μ_T-a.e., such that T(ω) = ∫_U ⟨ω(x), T⃗(x)⟩ dμ_T(x); μ_T is characterized by μ_T(W) = M_W(T) = sup_{ω ∈ D^n(U), |ω| ≤ 1, spt ω ⊆ W} T(ω) for any open W with closure a compact subset of U’ (printed with n in place of our k). The printed argument is expanded below (extension of T to continuous forms, the mass formula (2.8), a Borel version of T⃗); part (ii) adds the identification of an arbitrary measure μ with IsMassMeasure T μ with μ_T (uniqueness of measures that agree on a generating π-system). Throughout, |·| is the Euclidean coefficient norm of Simon 6, Remark 2.6: covectorEuclideanNorm on covectors (the norm used in massOn) and its dual norm on k-vectors.

1. Coordinates and norms. Let I := I(k,P) be the set of strictly increasing α : {1,…,k} → {1,…,P} (SimonMultiIndex k P), N := #I = binom(P,k), e_α := (e_{α(1)},…,e_{α(k)}) and dx^α := dx^{α(1)}∧⋯∧dx^{α(k)} (wedgeCovectors k (proj ∘ α)). By the determinant formula (wedgeCovectors_apply_det), dx^α(e_β) = δ_{αβ} for α, β ∈ I. A k-covector φ (continuous alternating k-linear form) is determined by its values on increasing tuples of basis vectors, hence φ = Σ_{α∈I} φ(e_α) dx^α and |φ| = (Σ_α φ(e_α)²)^{1/2} = covectorEuclideanNorm φ. Put c(φ) := (φ(e_α))_{α∈I} ∈ ℝ^N; c is a linear isometric bijection from (k-covectors, |·|) onto Euclidean ℝ^N. For a k-vector w (continuous linear functional on k-covectors) put w_α := w(dx^α) = euclideanNVectorCoordinate w α and |w| := (Σ_α w_α²)^{1/2}. Then w(φ) = Σ_α φ(e_α) w_α = ⟨c(φ), (w_α)_α⟩, so |w(φ)| ≤ |φ| |w|, and w ↦ (w_α)_α is a linear bijection onto ℝ^N.

2. Degenerate case N = 0 (k > P). Then every k-covector is 0, every test form is 0, T = 0 and M_W(T) = 0 for all W. The zero measure satisfies IsMassMeasure T 0, proving (i). If μ satisfies IsMassMeasure T μ, then μ(W) = 0 for every open W ⊂⊂ U and μ(ℝ^P∖U) = 0; as U is a countable union of such W (step 3), μ = 0, and ξ :≡ 0 satisfies (ii) (the a.e. condition is vacuous for the zero measure and T(ω) = 0 = ∫ 0 dμ). From now on N ≥ 1.

3. Exhaustion. U is open in ℝ^P, hence locally compact and σ-compact: there are compact K_q with ⋃_q K_q = U and, by local compactness, open W_q with K_q ⊆ W_q ⊆ closure(W_q) ⊆ U and closure(W_q) compact; replacing W_q by W_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ W_q we may assume W_q ↑. Each W_q is open and W_q ⊂⊂ U (CompactlyContainedOpen), U = ⋃_q W_q, every compact K ⊆ U lies in some W_q (finitely many W_q cover K), and M_{W_q}(T) < ∞.

4. Mass bound. If W ⊂⊂ U is open, ω ∈ D^k(U), tsupport ω ⊆ W and s := sup_x |ω(x)| > 0, then ±ω/s are admissible in the definition of M_W(T) (massOn: smooth test forms with tsupport in W and |·| ≤ 1 everywhere), so |T(ω)| ≤ s·M_W(T). If s = 0 then ω = 0 and T(ω) = 0.

5. Extension to continuous forms. Let K^k(U) be the space of continuous k-forms g on ℝ^P whose support is a compact subset of U; via c it is C_c(U, ℝ^N). Given g, choose an open W ⊂⊂ U containing spt g and a standard mollifier ϕ_σ (smooth, ≥ 0, ∫ϕ_σ = 1, spt ϕ_σ ⊆ B_σ(0)). For σ < dist(spt g, ℝ^P∖W) the coefficientwise convolution g_σ := ϕ_σ * g is a smooth form with compact support in W (so g_σ ∈ D^k(U) and tsupport g_σ ⊆ W), |g_σ(x)| ≤ sup|g| (g_σ(x) is an average of values of g and |·| is a norm), and g_σ → g uniformly as σ ↓ 0. By step 4, |T(g_σ) − T(g_{σ′})| ≤ M_W(T) sup|g_σ − g_{σ′}| → 0, so L(g) := lim_{σ↓0} T(g_σ) exists; by step 4 again it does not depend on W or on the smooth approximations supported in a fixed W ⊂⊂ U. L is linear; L(ω) = T(ω) for ω ∈ D^k(U) (|T(ω_σ) − T(ω)| ≤ M_W(T) sup|ω_σ − ω| → 0); and |L(g)| ≤ M_W(T) sup|g| whenever spt g ⊆ W ⊂⊂ U. In particular, for each compact K ⊆ U (say K ⊆ W_q), sup{L(g) : g ∈ K^k(U), |g| ≤ 1, spt g ⊆ K} ≤ M_{W_q}(T) < ∞.

6. Riesz representation (Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 4.14, with X := U, a locally compact Hausdorff space, and H := ℝ^N; SimonGMT simon_theorem_4_14_caratheodory, with the local boundedness hypothesis hL supplied by step 5). Let μ_T := vectorFunctionalEnvelopeMeasure L hL, a Radon measure on U. There is a Carathéodory-measurable ν : U → ℝ^N with |ν| = 1 μ_T-a.e. and L(g) = ∫_U ⟨c(g(x)), ν(x)⟩ dμ_T(x) for all g ∈ K^k(U), the integral being taken for the completion radonCaratheodoryMeasure μ_T. Moreover, by SimonGMT simon_theorem_4_14_positive_envelope (the equality (†) in the printed proof of 4.14), ∫ f dμ_T = λ(f) := sup{L(g) : g ∈ K^k(U), |g| ≤ f} for every f ∈ C_c(U, [0,∞)). Hence for every open W ⊆ U:
 μ_T(W) = sup{∫ f dμ_T : f ∈ C_c(W), 0 ≤ f ≤ 1} = sup{λ(f) : f ∈ C_c(W), 0 ≤ f ≤ 1} = sup{L(g) : g ∈ K^k(U), |g| ≤ 1, spt g ⊆ W};
 the first equality is inner regularity of Radon measures on open sets together with Urysohn's lemma; for the last, |g| ≤ f ≤ 1 with spt f ⊆ W gives |g| ≤ 1 and spt g ⊆ W, and conversely, for |g| ≤ 1 with compact spt g ⊆ W, Urysohn's lemma gives f ∈ C_c(W) with 0 ≤ f ≤ 1 and f = 1 on spt g, so |g| ≤ f.

7. Mass identity (2.8). Let W ⊂⊂ U be open. Every form ω admissible for M_W(T) lies in K^k(U) with |ω| ≤ 1 and spt ω ⊆ W, and L(ω) = T(ω); hence M_W(T) ≤ μ_T(W) (massOn is the supremum of ofReal(T(ω)) over admissible ω; since ω = 0 is admissible this is the supremum of the T(ω)). Conversely, for g ∈ K^k(U) with |g| ≤ 1 and spt g ⊆ W, the forms g_σ of step 5 (σ < dist(spt g, ℝ^P∖W)) are admissible for M_W(T) and T(g_σ) → L(g), so L(g) ≤ M_W(T). By step 6, μ_T(W) = M_W(T).

8. Proof of (i). Define the Borel measure μ₀ on ℝ^P by μ₀(A) := μ_T(A ∩ U). Then μ₀(ℝ^P∖U) = 0, and μ₀(W) = μ_T(W) = M_W(T) for every open W ⊂⊂ U by step 7. Hence IsMassMeasure T μ₀.

9. Uniqueness. Let μ be any Borel measure on ℝ^P with IsMassMeasure T μ. Let 𝒞 := {W : W open, W ⊂⊂ U} ∪ {A : A Borel, A ∩ U = ∅}. 𝒞 is closed under finite intersections: W₁ ∩ W₂ is open with closure contained in the compact set closure(W₁) ⊆ U; W ∩ A = ∅, and ∅ is an open set ⊂⊂ U; (A ∩ A′) ∩ U = ∅. 𝒞 generates the Borel σ-algebra: every open O equals (O∖U) ∪ ⋃_q (O ∩ W_q), where O∖U ∈ 𝒞 and each O ∩ W_q is open and ⊂⊂ U. μ and μ₀ agree on 𝒞 (both equal M_W(T) on open W ⊂⊂ U and both vanish on Borel subsets of ℝ^P∖U). The sets W_q (q ∈ ℕ) and ℝ^P∖U belong to 𝒞, have finite μ-measure (M_{W_q}(T) < ∞, resp. 0) and cover ℝ^P. By the uniqueness theorem for measures agreeing on a generating π-system with such a cover (Mathlib Measure.ext_of_generateFrom_of_iUnion), μ = μ₀. In particular μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ U.

10. The field ξ. Since ν is μ_T-measurable with values in ℝ^N, there is a Borel map ν̃ : ℝ^P → ℝ^N with ν̃ = ν μ_T-a.e. on U. Redefine ν̃(x) := (1, 0, …, 0) on the Borel set (ℝ^P∖U) ∪ {x : |ν̃(x)| ≠ 1}; the new ν̃ is Borel, |ν̃| ≡ 1, and still ν̃ = ν μ_T-a.e. on U (because |ν| = 1 μ_T-a.e.). Define ξ(x) ∈ Λ_k(ℝ^P) by ξ(x)(φ) := ⟨c(φ), ν̃(x)⟩ = Σ_α φ(e_α) ν̃_α(x). The map x ↦ ξ(x) is Borel into the finite-dimensional normed space Λ_k(ℝ^P) (its coordinates are Borel), hence strongly measurable; and ξ(x)(dx^α) = ν̃_α(x), since c(dx^α) is the α-th unit vector, so Σ_α (euclideanNVectorCoordinate (ξ x) α)² = |ν̃(x)|² = 1 for every x, in particular for μ-a.e. x.

11. Representation. Let ω ∈ D^k(U); its support is a compact subset of U, contained in some W_q. The function x ↦ ξ(x)(ω(x)) = ⟨c(ω(x)), ν̃(x)⟩ is Borel, bounded by sup|ω|, and vanishes outside spt ω, which has finite μ-measure (step 9); so it is μ-integrable. By steps 5, 6 and 9, and since ω vanishes outside U: T(ω) = L(ω) = ∫_U ⟨c(ω(x)), ν(x)⟩ dμ_T(x) = ∫_U ⟨c(ω(x)), ν̃(x)⟩ dμ_T(x) = ∫_{ℝ^P} ξ(x)(ω(x)) dμ₀(x) = ∫ ξ(x)(ω(x)) dμ(x). Thus IsMeasureRepresentation T μ ξ, which together with step 10 proves (ii). ∎
proof_key_steps: Identify k-covectors with ℝ^N isometrically via φ ↦ (φ(e_α))_α (covectorEuclideanNorm) and k-vectors via w ↦ (w(dx^α))_α; the case k > P gives T = 0 and μ = 0.
The mass bound |T(ω)| ≤ sup|ω|·M_W(T) and mollification extend T to a locally bounded linear functional L on continuous compactly supported forms in U.
Simon Ch. 1, 4.14 (vector Riesz) gives a Radon measure μ_T on U and a unit field ν with L(g) = ∫⟨c(g), ν⟩dμ_T and μ_T(W) = sup{L(g) : |g| ≤ 1, spt g ⊆ W}.
Mollification shows this supremum equals M_W(T) for open W ⊂⊂ U, so μ₀ := μ_T(· ∩ U) satisfies IsMassMeasure T μ₀.
Any μ with IsMassMeasure T μ equals μ₀: both agree on the π-system of open W ⊂⊂ U and Borel sets missing U, which generates the Borel sets and has a countable finite-measure cover.
A Borel unit version ν̃ of ν defines a strongly measurable ξ with Σ_α ξ(x)(dx^α)² = 1, and T(ω) = ∫ξ(ω)dμ with μ-integrable integrand.

subproblem.title: Mickle-Radó density dichotomy (Mattila 18.5)
subproblem.statement: Let m ∈ ℕ, k := m + 1, and let ψ be an outer measure on ℝᵏ (ψ(∅) = 0, monotone, countably subadditive) with ψ(B(c,τ)) = sup_{0<τ′<τ}ψ(B(c,τ′)) for all c ∈ ℝᵏ and τ ∈ ℝ (B open balls). Let D ⊆ ℝᵏ be a Borel set with ψ(D) = 0, and for c ∈ ℝᵏ let ϑ(c) := limsup_{t↓0}ψ(B(c,t))/tᵏ ∈ [0,∞]. Then the set {c ∈ D : 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞} has Lebesgue measure zero.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (m : ℕ) (ψ : OuterMeasure (Eucl (m + 1))) (D : Set (Eucl (m + 1))), (∀ (c : Eucl (m + 1)) (τ : ℝ), ψ (ball c τ) = ⨆ τ' ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) τ, ψ (ball c τ')) → MeasurableSet D → ψ D = 0 → (volume : Measure (Eucl (m + 1))) {c | c ∈ D ∧ 0 < limsup (fun t : ℝ => ψ (ball c t) / ENNReal.ofReal (t ^ (m + 1))) (𝓝[>] 0) ∧ limsup (fun t : ℝ => ψ (ball c t) / ENNReal.ofReal (t ^ (m + 1))) (𝓝[>] 0) < ⊤} = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: P. Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces, Theorem 18.5. This is a density theorem of Mickle and Radó: if ψ is a measure on ℝᵏ and A is Lᵏ-measurable with ψ(A) = 0, then for Lᵏ-a.e. x ∈ A, limsup_{r↓0}r^{−k}ψ(B(x,r)) ∈ {0,∞}. It is the version cited by Hovila-Järvenpää-Järvenpää-Ledrappier (arXiv:1104.3453, proof of Lemma 2.4); see also P. Mattila, Rectifiability: a survey (arXiv:2112.00540), Lemma 4.14 ('a simple covering argument combined with Lebesgue density theorem'). That argument is written out below. The inner continuity of ψ on open balls is used only to make the sets involved Borel.

Notation: B(c,τ) is the open ball in ℝᵏ, k := m + 1, ω_k := Lᵏ(B(0,1)), f_c(t) := ψ(B(c,t))/tᵏ for t > 0, and ϑ(c) = limsup_{t↓0}f_c(t).

1. Measurability. For τ > 0 the map c ↦ ψ(B(c,τ)) is lower semicontinuous. Indeed, let c_l → c and 0 < τ′ < τ. Then B(c,τ′) ⊆ B(c_l,τ) as soon as |c_l − c| < τ − τ′, so ψ(B(c,τ′)) ≤ liminf_lψ(B(c_l,τ)). Taking the supremum over τ′ ∈ (0,τ) and using the hypothesis ψ(B(c,τ)) = sup_{τ′<τ}ψ(B(c,τ′)) gives ψ(B(c,τ)) ≤ liminf_lψ(B(c_l,τ)).
 For q ∈ ℕ, q ≥ 1, let g_q(c) := sup_{0<t<1/q}f_c(t). As a supremum of lower semicontinuous functions, g_q is lower semicontinuous, hence Borel. Moreover g_q ↓ ϑ pointwise as q → ∞, since ϑ(c) = inf_qg_q(c) by the definition of limsup. Hence ϑ is Borel.

2. Reduction. For q ≥ 1 let S_q := {c ∈ D : ϑ(c) > 1/q and g_q(c) ≤ q}. This is a Borel set, since {g_q ≤ q} is closed.
 Let c ∈ D with 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞. Since inf_qg_q(c) < ∞, g_{q₀}(c) < ∞ for some q₀, and g_q is non-increasing in q. So every q ≥ max(q₀, g_{q₀}(c)) with 1/q < ϑ(c) satisfies c ∈ S_q.
 Hence {c ∈ D : 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞} ⊆ ⋃_qS_q, and it suffices to show Lᵏ(S_q) = 0 for each q.

3. Lᵏ(S_q) = 0. Fix q and suppose Lᵏ(S_q) > 0.
 By inner regularity of Lebesgue measure there is a compact K ⊆ S_q with Lᵏ(K) > 0. Lebesgue's density theorem (Mathlib Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div) gives Lᵏ(K ∩ B̄(c,ρ))/Lᵏ(B̄(c,ρ)) → 1 as ρ ↓ 0 for (Lᵏ⌞K)-a.e. c. Since Lᵏ(K) > 0, such a point c₀ ∈ K exists. Since Lᵏ(∂B(c₀,ρ)) = 0, Lᵏ(B(c₀,ρ)∖K)/Lᵏ(B(c₀,ρ)) = 1 − Lᵏ(K ∩ B̄(c₀,ρ))/Lᵏ(B̄(c₀,ρ)) → 0 as ρ ↓ 0.
 Let ε := 1/(2q²12ᵏ). Choose t₀ > 0 with Lᵏ(B(c₀,2t)∖K) ≤ εω_k(2t)ᵏ for 0 < t < t₀, and with 12ε^{1/k}t₀ < 1/q. Since c₀ ∈ S_q, ϑ(c₀) > 1/q, so there is t ∈ (0,t₀) with ψ(B(c₀,t)) > tᵏ/q.
 Because K ⊆ S_q ⊆ D and ψ(D) = 0, ψ(K) = 0, so ψ(B(c₀,t)) ≤ ψ(B(c₀,t)∖K) + ψ(K) = ψ(B(c₀,t)∖K).
 For z ∈ B(c₀,t)∖K let d(z) := dist(z,K). Since K is closed and c₀ ∈ K, 0 < d(z) ≤ |z − c₀| < t. The open ball B(z,d(z)) does not meet K and is contained in B(c₀,2t). Hence ω_kd(z)ᵏ ≤ Lᵏ(B(c₀,2t)∖K) ≤ εω_k(2t)ᵏ, i.e. d(z) ≤ 2ε^{1/k}t.
 By the Vitali covering lemma (enlargement factor 2, as in Mathlib Vitali.exists_disjoint_subfamily_covering_enlargement) there are countably many points z_i ∈ B(c₀,t)∖K such that the balls B(z_i,d_i), d_i := d(z_i), are pairwise disjoint and B(c₀,t)∖K ⊆ ⋃_iB(z_i,5d_i).
 Since K is compact, choose z′_i ∈ K with |z_i − z′_i| = d_i. Then B(z_i,5d_i) ⊆ B(z′_i,6d_i) and 6d_i ≤ 12ε^{1/k}t < 1/q. So g_q(z′_i) ≤ q gives ψ(B(z′_i,6d_i)) ≤ q(6d_i)ᵏ. The disjoint balls B(z_i,d_i) lie in B(c₀,2t)∖K. Therefore
 ψ(B(c₀,t)∖K) ≤ Σ_iψ(B(z′_i,6d_i)) ≤ q6ᵏΣ_id_iᵏ = q6ᵏω_k^{−1}Σ_iLᵏ(B(z_i,d_i)) ≤ q6ᵏω_k^{−1}Lᵏ(B(c₀,2t)∖K) ≤ q6ᵏε(2t)ᵏ = tᵏ/(2q).
 This contradicts ψ(B(c₀,t)) > tᵏ/q. Hence Lᵏ(S_q) = 0, and Lᵏ({c ∈ D : 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞}) ≤ Σ_qLᵏ(S_q) = 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: Inner continuity on balls makes c ↦ ψ(B(c,τ)) lower semicontinuous, so g_q(c) = sup_{0<t<1/q}ψ(B(c,t))/tᵏ and ϑ = inf_q g_q are Borel.
{c ∈ D : 0 < ϑ(c) < ∞} ⊆ ⋃_q S_q, where the Borel sets S_q := {c ∈ D : ϑ(c) > 1/q, g_q(c) ≤ q} carry the uniform upper bound ψ(B(c,τ)) ≤ qτᵏ for τ < 1/q.
If Lᵏ(S_q) > 0, take a compact K ⊆ S_q and a Lebesgue density point c₀ ∈ K. Since ψ(K) ≤ ψ(D) = 0, ψ(B(c₀,t)) = ψ(B(c₀,t)∖K).

Cover B(c₀,t)∖K by Vitali balls B(z,dist(z,K)), whose radii are small because c₀ is a density point. The enlarged balls centred in K have ψ-mass ≤ q(6d)ᵏ, so ψ(B(c₀,t)) ≤ tᵏ/(2q), contradicting ϑ(c₀) > 1/q.

audit.reason: Ball continuity supplies the required Borel level sets. At a density point of a compact subset, the distance-to-set Vitali covering gives the explicit contradiction t^k/q < t^k/(2q). Only outer-measure properties are used, consistent with [Mattila, Lemma 4.14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.00540).

subproblem.title: Weighted approximate tangent spaces exist a.e. on a countably rectifiable set (Simon 3, Theorem 1.9 via Remark 1.8(1), localized to U)
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, n := m + 1, U ⊆ ℝ^P open, M ⊆ U Hⁿ-measurable (null-measurable for μHE[n]) and countably n-rectifiable, and θ : ℝ^P → ℝ with θ(x) > 0 for x ∈ M and θ Hⁿ-integrable on M ∩ K for every compact K ⊆ U. Then for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M there is an n-dimensional linear subspace V of ℝ^P which is the approximate tangent space of M at x with respect to θ (HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt n M θ x V): dim V = n and lim_{r↓0} ∫_{η_{x,r}(M)} f(y) θ(x + r y) dHⁿ(y) = θ(x) ∫_V f dHⁿ for every f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P), where η_{x,r}(y) = r^{-1}(y − x).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (U M : Set (Eucl P)) (θ : Eucl P → ℝ), IsOpen U → M ⊆ U → NullMeasurableSet M (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P)) → CountablyRectifiable (m + 1) M → (∀ x ∈ M, 0 < θ x) → (∀ K : Set (Eucl P), IsCompact K → K ⊆ U → IntegrableOn θ (M ∩ K) (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P))) → ∀ᵐ x ∂((μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P)).restrict M), ∃ V : Submodule ℝ (Eucl P), HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt (m + 1) M θ x V
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 3, Theorem 1.9 (p. 75): 'Suppose M ⊆ ℝ^{n+ℓ} is Hⁿ-measurable and θ is a positive Hⁿ-measurable function on M with ∫_{M∩K} θ dHⁿ < ∞ for each compact K ⊆ ℝ^{n+ℓ}. Then M is countably n-rectifiable ⟺ M has an approximate tangent space T_xM with respect to θ for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M'. Simon deduces this from Theorem 1.6 via Remark 1.8(1). We follow the printed proofs of 1.6 '⇒' (pp. 71-72) and of Remark 1.8(1), the latter using Lusin's Theorem 1.17 and 3.6 of Ch. 1. There are three adaptations.
 (a) θ is only integrable on compact subsets of U; this is handled by localization (step 2).
 (b) The printed proof of 1.6 '⇒' covers M by embedded C¹ submanifolds (Lemma 1.2). The 'only if' part of Lemma 1.2 rests on the C¹ approximation theorem (Ch. 2, 1.5), and it is not in the pinned library: SimonGMT Chapter03/SubmanifoldCover.lean proves only the converse. Step 4 does not use Lemma 1.2. It cuts the Lipschitz parametrizations of Definition 1.1 into bi-Lipschitz pieces and computes the blow-ups with the injective and linear area formulas, using only proved, axiom-checked library results (listed in step 4). The density argument of the printed proof (the Upper Density Theorem 3.6 of Ch. 1) is kept.
 (c) The case P = n needs no separate treatment, and P < n is vacuous (step 1).

1. Dimension. If P < n then Hⁿ ≡ 0 on ℝ^P (ℝ^P has Hausdorff dimension P < n), so Hⁿ⌞M = 0 and the statement is vacuous. Assume P ≥ n.

2. Localization. Let W_q (q ∈ ℕ) be open sets with closure(W_q) compact and ⊆ U and ⋃_q W_q = U, and let M_q := M ∩ W_q (Hⁿ-measurable). θ is Hⁿ-integrable on M_q ⊆ M ∩ closure(W_q), hence on M_q ∩ K for every compact K ⊆ ℝ^P. For x ∈ M_q, (M_q, θ) has approximate tangent space V at x iff (M, θ) has: if f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P), spt f ⊆ B_R(0) and 0 < r < dist(x, ℝ^P∖W_q)/R, then every y ∈ η_{x,r}(M)∖η_{x,r}(M_q) has x + r y ∈ M∖W_q, so r|y| ≥ dist(x, ℝ^P∖W_q) > rR and f(y) = 0; therefore ∫_{η_{x,r}(M)} f(y) θ(x + r y) dHⁿ(y) = ∫_{η_{x,r}(M_q)} f(y) θ(x + r y) dHⁿ(y) for all small r > 0, and the limits as r ↓ 0 coincide. Since M = ⋃_q M_q and a countable union of null sets is null, it suffices to prove the theorem for each M_q. Fix q and write M for M_q: now θ ∈ L¹(Hⁿ⌞M), θ > 0 on M, and M is Hⁿ-measurable and countably n-rectifiable.

3. Remark 1.8(1). Hⁿ⌞M is σ-finite: M = ⋃_k {x ∈ M : θ(x) > 1/k} and Hⁿ({θ > 1/k} ∩ M) ≤ k ∫_M θ dHⁿ < ∞. By Lusin's theorem (Simon Ch. 1, 1.17) applied to θ on these sets of finite measure, and the pasting lemma for finitely many closed sets, there is an increasing sequence of closed sets M^{(j)} ⊆ M, compact because M ⊆ W_q is bounded (Lusin: SimonGMT IsBorelRegularOuterMeasure.simon_theorem_1_17; θ|M is Hⁿ-Carathéodory-measurable, being Hⁿ⌞M-a.e. equal to a Borel function), with Hⁿ(M∖⋃_j M^{(j)}) = 0 and θ|M^{(j)} continuous; then θ ≥ c_j > 0 on M^{(j)} and Hⁿ(M^{(j)}) ≤ c_j^{-1} ∫_M θ < ∞. Let μ := θ Hⁿ⌞M (a finite Borel regular measure). By the Upper Density Theorem (Simon Ch. 1, 3.6), applied to μ and the μ-measurable set M∖M^{(j)} of finite μ-measure, there is an Hⁿ-null set E_j such that Θ*ⁿ(μ, M∖M^{(j)}, x) = 0 for every x ∈ M^{(j)}∖E_j.

4. Theorem 1.6 '⇒' for M′ := M^{(j)}, via Lipschitz parametrizations. M′ is compact, Hⁿ(M′) < ∞, and M′ is countably n-rectifiable as a subset of M. Claim: there is an Hⁿ-null set Z_j ⊆ ℝ^P such that every x ∈ M′∖Z_j has two properties. First, there is an n-dimensional subspace L_x with lim_{λ↓0}∫_{η_{x,λ}(M′)}f dHⁿ = ∫_{L_x}f dHⁿ for every f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P) (Definition 1.4 of Ch. 3). Second, Hⁿ(M′ ∩ B̄_ρ(x)) ≤ C_xρⁿ for all small ρ > 0.

subproblem.title: Besicovitch-Federer trichotomy for almost every linear map (Mattila 18.9)
subproblem.statement: Let N, m ∈ ℕ, k := m + 1, Hᵏ := μHE[k], let E ⊆ ℝ^N be σ-compact with Hᵏ(E) < ∞, and let δ > 0. For v = (v₁, …, v_k) ∈ (ℝ^N)^k let L_v(x) := (⟨v₁,x⟩, …, ⟨v_k,x⟩), let X_v(a,r,s) := {x : |x − a| < r, |L_v(x − a)| < s|x − a|}, and let ν_v := (L_v)_#(Hᵏ⌞E), a finite Borel measure on ℝᵏ. Then for Lebesgue-a.e. v ∈ (ℝ^N)^k and Hᵏ-a.e. a ∈ E, at least one of the following holds. (T1) For every η > 0 there is s ∈ (0,1) with Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(a,r,s)) ≤ η(rs)ᵏ for all r ∈ (0,δ). (T2) The upper k-density of ν_v at L_va is infinite (dimensionalUpperDensity ν_v k univ (L_v a) = ∞). (T3) Some x ∈ E with x ≠ a and |x − a| < δ has L_vx = L_va.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: P. Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces, Lemma 18.9. We use the version for transversal families of maps in R. Hovila, E. Järvenpää, M. Järvenpää and F. Ledrappier, Geom. Dedicata 161 (2012), arXiv:1104.3453, Lemma 2.4, whose alternatives (2.1)/(2.2)/(2.3) are (T1)/(T2)/(T3) here and whose proof is followed. The family is {L_v : v ∈ (ℝ^N)^k}, parametrized by the row vectors v. For it, the k-dimensional slices of the parameter space used in that proof are the affine families v ⊕_j c (c ∈ ℝᵏ) defined below, and the comparison between cones and unions of fibres becomes the exact inclusions (i), (ii) of step 4. The Mickle-Radó theorem used there ([Ma, 18.5]) is the sibling mickle_rado.

Notation: k := m + 1, Hᵏ := μHE[k], and μ := Hᵏ⌞E, i.e. μ(S) := Hᵏ(E ∩ S). Since E is σ-compact (hence Borel) and Hᵏ(E) < ∞, μ is a finite Borel measure on ℝ^N with Hᵏ(E ∩ S) = μ(S) for Borel S. X_v(a,r,s) is an open set not containing a. Further, F(a,v,s) := sup_{0<r<δ}(rs)^{−k}μ(X_v(a,r,s)), Φ(a,v) := limsup_{s↓0}F(a,v,s) ∈ [0,∞], and ℒ denotes Lebesgue measure on (ℝ^N)^k ≅ ℝ^{kN}.

1. Reduction to Φ ∈ {0,∞}. Let a ∈ E.
 If Φ(a,v) = 0, then (T1) holds. Given η > 0, F(a,v,s) < η for all small s > 0; pick such an s ∈ (0,1). Then for r ∈ (0,δ), Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(a,r,s)) = μ(X_v(a,r,s)) ≤ F(a,v,s)(rs)ᵏ ≤ η(rs)ᵏ.
 If Φ(a,v) = ∞, then (T2) holds. Given Λ > 0 and ρ₀ > 0, there is s ∈ (0,ρ₀/δ) with F(a,v,s) > Λ, hence some r ∈ (0,δ) with μ(X_v(a,r,s)) > Λ(rs)ᵏ. Put ρ := rs < ρ₀. Every x ∈ X_v(a,r,s) has |L_vx − L_va| < s|x − a| < ρ. So ν_v(B̄(L_va,ρ)) ≥ μ(L_v^{−1}(B(L_va,ρ))) ≥ μ(X_v(a,r,s)) > Λρᵏ. Thus the density quotient ν_v(univ ∩ B̄(L_va,ρ))/(ω_kρᵏ) of dimensionalUpperDensity exceeds Λ/ω_k for arbitrarily small ρ > 0, so dimensionalUpperDensity ν_v k univ (L_va) = ∞.
 Hence it suffices to show: for ℒ-a.e. v and μ-a.e. a, either Φ(a,v) ∈ {0,∞} or (T3) holds. If N = 0, then ℝ^N is a point, X_v(a,r,s) = ∅, Φ ≡ 0, and (T1) always holds; so assume N ≥ 1 from now on.

2. Measurability.
 (a) The set {(x,a,v) : |x − a| < r, |L_v(x − a)| < s|x − a|} is open in ℝ^N × ℝ^N × (ℝ^N)^k. By Fatou's lemma, (a,v) ↦ μ(X_v(a,r,s)) is lower semicontinuous, hence Borel.
 (b) For fixed (a,v,s), r ↦ μ(X_v(a,r,s)) is nondecreasing and left continuous, because X_v(a,r,s) = ⋃_{r′<r}X_v(a,r′,s). So the supremum defining F may be taken over rational r ∈ (0,δ), and F is Borel in (a,v).
 (c) If 0 < s ≤ s′, then X_v(a,r,s) ⊆ X_v(a,r,s′), hence F(a,v,s) ≤ (s′/s)ᵏF(a,v,s′). Therefore the limsup defining Φ may be taken along rational s: for s_l ↓ 0 choose rational s′_l ∈ (s_l, s_l(1 + 1/l)). So Φ is Borel.
 (d) Write E = ⋃_iK_i with each K_i compact. The set T3 := {(a,v) : some x ∈ E has 0 < |x − a| < δ and L_v(x − a) = 0} is the union over i, l ∈ ℕ of the projections to (a,v) of the compact sets {(x,a,v) : x ∈ K_i, 1/l ≤ |x − a| ≤ δ − 1/l, |a| ≤ l, |v| ≤ l, L_v(x − a) = 0}. So T3 is σ-compact, hence Borel.
 Hence 𝔅 := {(a,v) : 0 < Φ(a,v) < ∞}∖T3 is Borel.

3. Fixed a: slices and Mickle-Radó. Fix a ∈ ℝ^N; we show ℒ({v : (a,v) ∈ 𝔅}) = 0.
 For j ∈ {1, …, N}, w ∈ (ℝ^N)^k and c ∈ ℝᵏ let w ⊕_j c := (w₁ + c₁e_j, …, w_k + c_ke_j). Then L_{w⊕_jc}(y) = L_w(y) + y_jc, where y_j := ⟨e_j,y⟩, and (w ⊕_j c) ⊕_j c′ = w ⊕_j (c + c′). For C ⊆ ℝᵏ let
 K_{j,w}(C) := {x ≠ a : L_{w⊕_jc}(x − a) = 0 for some c ∈ C} and ψ_{j,w}(C) := sup_{0<r<δ}r^{−k}Hᵏ(E ∩ B(a,r) ∩ K_{j,w}(C)).
 (a) ψ_{j,w} is an outer measure on ℝᵏ. It vanishes on ∅ and is monotone. Since K_{j,w}(⋃_iC_i) = ⋃_iK_{j,w}(C_i) and Hᵏ is countably subadditive, each set function C ↦ r^{−k}Hᵏ(E ∩ B(a,r) ∩ K_{j,w}(C)) is countably subadditive, and so is their supremum.
 (b) Let τ > 0. Solving L_w(x − a) + (x − a)_jc′ = 0 for c′ shows that K_{j,w}(B(c,τ)) = {x : |L_{w⊕_jc}(x − a)| < τ|(x − a)_j|} ∪ {x ≠ a : (x − a)_j = 0, L_w(x − a) = 0}, a Borel set. Also K_{j,w}(B(c,τ)) = ⋃_{τ′<τ}K_{j,w}(B(c,τ′)), an increasing union. By continuity from below of μ and interchanging suprema, ψ_{j,w}(B(c,τ)) = sup_{0<τ′<τ}ψ_{j,w}(B(c,τ′)). For τ ≤ 0 both sides are 0. Moreover K_{j,w}(B(c,t)) = K_{j,w⊕_jc}(B(0,t)), hence ψ_{j,w}(B(c,t)) = ψ_{j,w⊕_jc}(B(0,t)).
 (c) Let D_{j,w} := {c ∈ ℝᵏ : (T3) fails at (a, w ⊕_j c)}, i.e. the set of c for which no x ∈ E has 0 < |x − a| < δ and L_{w⊕_jc}(x − a) = 0. It is Borel, since its complement is the preimage of the Borel set T3 (step 2(d)) under the continuous map c ↦ (a, w ⊕_j c). Moreover ψ_{j,w}(D_{j,w}) = 0: for r < δ, any point of E ∩ B(a,r) ∩ K_{j,w}(D_{j,w}) would witness (T3) at some (a, w ⊕_j c) with c ∈ D_{j,w}.
 (d) Apply the sibling mickle_rado with ψ := ψ_{j,w} and D := D_{j,w}; its hypotheses are (a)-(c). It gives: for Lᵏ-a.e. c ∈ D_{j,w}, ϑ_{j,w}(c) := limsup_{t↓0}ψ_{j,w}(B(c,t))/tᵏ ∈ {0,∞}. By (b), ϑ_{j,w}(c) = ϑ_j(w ⊕_j c), where ϑ_j(u) := limsup_{t↓0}ψ_{j,u}(B(0,t))/tᵏ. Also c ∈ D_{j,w} iff (T3) fails at (a, w ⊕_j c).
 (e) The function u ↦ ϑ_j(u) is Borel. By (b), the set {(x,u) : x ∈ B(a,r) ∩ K_{j,u}(B(0,t))} is Borel in ℝ^N × (ℝ^N)^k, so u ↦ μ(B(a,r) ∩ K_{j,u}(B(0,t))) is Borel (Tonelli). The supremum over r may be taken over rationals (left continuity in r), and the limsup over t along rationals (monotonicity in t, as in 2(c)).
 Hence 𝔅_j := {u : (T3) fails at (a,u) and 0 < ϑ_j(u) < ∞} is Borel. Let W_j be the set of w ∈ (ℝ^N)^k whose rows have zero j-th coordinate. The map (w,c) ↦ w ⊕_j c identifies W_j × ℝᵏ with (ℝ^N)^k; it is a linear isomorphism that permutes coordinates, so ℒ is the product of the Lebesgue measures. For each w ∈ W_j, {c : w ⊕_j c ∈ 𝔅_j} = {c ∈ D_{j,w} : 0 < ϑ_{j,w}(c) < ∞}, which is Lᵏ-null by (d). By Fubini, ℒ(𝔅_j) = 0.

4. Cones versus unions of fibres. For every u ∈ (ℝ^N)^k, r ∈ (0,δ) and s > 0:
 (i) X_u(a,r,s) ⊆ ⋃_{j=1}^N(B(a,r) ∩ K_{j,u}(B(0,√N s))). Indeed, let x ∈ X_u(a,r,s); then x ≠ a. Choose j with |(x − a)_j| ≥ |x − a|/√N and put c := −L_u(x − a)/(x − a)_j. Then |c| < s|x − a|·√N/|x − a| = √N s, and L_{u⊕_jc}(x − a) = L_u(x − a) + (x − a)_jc = 0.
 (ii) B(a,r) ∩ K_{j,u}(B(0,s)) ⊆ X_u(a,r,s) for each j. Indeed, if x ≠ a, |x − a| < r and L_{u⊕_jc}(x − a) = 0 with |c| < s, then |L_u(x − a)| = |c||(x − a)_j| ≤ |c||x − a| < s|x − a|.
 By (ii), ψ_{j,u}(B(0,s)) ≤ sup_rr^{−k}μ(X_u(a,r,s)) = sᵏF(a,u,s), so ϑ_j(u) ≤ Φ(a,u).
 By (i) and subadditivity, (rs)^{−k}μ(X_u(a,r,s)) ≤ s^{−k}Σ_jψ_{j,u}(B(0,√N s)). Hence F(a,u,s) ≤ N^{k/2}Σ_jψ_{j,u}(B(0,√N s))/(√N s)ᵏ and Φ(a,u) ≤ N^{k/2}Σ_jϑ_j(u).
 Consequently, suppose (T3) fails at (a,u) and u ∉ ⋃_j𝔅_j. Then each ϑ_j(u) ∈ {0,∞}. If some ϑ_j(u) = ∞, then Φ(a,u) = ∞; otherwise Φ(a,u) = 0. Thus {u : (a,u) ∈ 𝔅} ⊆ ⋃_j𝔅_j, which is ℒ-null by 3(e).

5. Fubini in (a,v). 𝔅 is Borel (step 2) and every section {v : (a,v) ∈ 𝔅} is ℒ-null (step 4). So (μ ⊗ ℒ)(𝔅) = 0, and by Fubini, for ℒ-a.e. v the section {a : (a,v) ∈ 𝔅} is μ-null. For such v and μ-a.e. a, i.e. for a.e. a with respect to μHE[k] restricted to E, either Φ(a,v) ∈ {0,∞} or (T3) holds. Step 1 then gives (T1) ∨ (T2) ∨ (T3). ∎
proof_key_steps: Φ(a,v) = 0 gives (T1). Φ(a,v) = ∞ gives an infinite projected density (T2), since X_v(a,r,s) ⊆ L_v⁻¹(B(L_va, rs)).
All functions and sets involved are Borel (semicontinuity, reduction to rationals, σ-compact projections), so Fubini applies.

Fix a. Along each slice w ⊕_j c (c ∈ ℝᵏ), the outer measure ψ_{j,w}(C) = sup_r r⁻ᵏHᵏ(E ∩ B(a,r) ∩ ⋃_{c∈C}fibres) vanishes on the 'fibre not hit' set. So mickle_rado gives slice densities in {0,∞} a.e., and Fubini over the remaining coordinates extends this to a.e. matrix.
Exact inclusions between the cones X_u(a,r,s) and the fibre unions over B(0,s), resp. B(0,√N s), give ϑ_j ≤ Φ ≤ N^{k/2}Σ_jϑ_j, so Φ ∈ {0,∞} unless (T3) holds.
Fubini on Hᵏ⌞E ⊗ ℒ turns 'for every a, a.e. v' into 'for a.e. v, a.e. a'.

subproblem.title: Blow-up orientation: ξ orients the weighted approximate tangent spaces when ∂T has locally finite mass (Simon 6, proof of 8.1, (10)-(13))
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, n := m + 1, U ⊆ ℝ^P open, and T ∈ D_n(U) with M_W(∂T) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U. Let M ⊆ U be Hⁿ-measurable and countably n-rectifiable, θ : ℝ^P → ℝ with θ > 0 on M and θ Hⁿ-integrable on M ∩ K for every compact K ⊆ U, and ξ : ℝ^P → Λ_n(ℝ^P) Hⁿ⌞M-measurable with Euclidean coefficient norm 1 Hⁿ-a.e. on M (Σ_{α∈I(n,P)} ξ(x)(dx^α)² = 1), and suppose T(ω) = ∫_M θ(x) ⟨ω(x), ξ(x)⟩ dHⁿ(x) (= tauAction n M θ ξ ω) for every ω ∈ Dⁿ(U). Then for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ M there is an orthonormal n-tuple τ = (τ₁, …, τ_n) in ℝ^P such that span{τ₁, …, τ_n} is the approximate tangent space of M at x with respect to θ and ξ(x) = τ₁∧⋯∧τ_n or ξ(x) = −τ₁∧⋯∧τ_n (simpleNVector τ).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)), IsOpen U → ∀ T : GeometricCurrentOn U (m + 1), (∀ W, CompactlyContainedOpen W U → T.boundary.massOn W < ∞) → ∀ (M : Set (Eucl P)) (θ : Eucl P → ℝ) (ξ : Eucl P → NVector (Eucl P) (m + 1)), M ⊆ U → NullMeasurableSet M (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P)) → CountablyRectifiable (m + 1) M → (∀ x ∈ M, 0 < θ x) → (∀ K : Set (Eucl P), IsCompact K → K ⊆ U → IntegrableOn θ (M ∩ K) (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P))) → AEStronglyMeasurable ξ ((μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P)).restrict M) → (∀ᵐ x ∂((μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P)).restrict M), ∑ α : SimonMultiIndex (m + 1) P, (euclideanNVectorCoordinate (ξ x) α) ^ 2 = 1) → (∀ ω : TestFormOn U (m + 1), T ω = tauAction (m + 1) M θ ξ ω) → ∀ᵐ x ∂((μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P)).restrict M), ∃ τ : Fin (m + 1) → Eucl P, Orthonormal ℝ τ ∧ HasWeightedApproximateTangentSpaceAt (m + 1) M θ x (Submodule.span ℝ (range τ)) ∧ (ξ x = simpleNVector τ ∨ ξ x = -simpleNVector τ)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, proof of Theorem 8.1 (pp. 174-175), displays (10)-(13) and the concluding argument (‘We now claim that (13), taken together with the fact that ∂S_x = 0, implies that ξ(x) orients L …’), in the form of the parent proof's Steps 5-7: the printed derivation of (11) through C¹ submanifolds N_j and (10) is replaced, as in the parent proof, by the existence of weighted approximate tangent spaces (sibling weighted_tangent_ae, i.e. Ch. 3, 1.9) and Lebesgue points of ξ with respect to θHⁿ⌞M; (12) uses finiteness of the upper density of the mass measure of ∂T (printed (3)), obtained here from the siblings mass_measure_representation and density_comparison. Norms |·| are the Euclidean coefficient norms of Simon 6, Remark 2.6, so |⟨φ, w⟩| ≤ |φ| |w|; Hⁿ = μHE[n]; Θ*ⁿ(λ, x) := limsup_{r↓0} λ(B̄_r(x))/(ω_n rⁿ) for a measure λ.

1. Preliminaries. If P < n then Hⁿ ≡ 0 on ℝ^P and there is nothing to prove; assume P ≥ n. Let μ := θHⁿ⌞M, i.e. μ(A) := ∫_{A∩M} θ dHⁿ. μ is a Borel measure on ℝ^P with μ(ℝ^P∖U) = 0 and μ(K) < ∞ for compact K ⊆ U. Since θ > 0 on M, Hⁿ⌞M ≪ μ (if μ(A) = 0 for a Borel A then θ = 0 Hⁿ-a.e. on A ∩ M, so Hⁿ(A ∩ M) = 0); also μ ≪ Hⁿ⌞M, so ξ is μ-measurable and |ξ| = 1 μ-a.e. Let W_q (q ∈ ℕ) be open sets ⊂⊂ U with ⋃_q W_q = U. By the sibling mass_measure_representation applied to ∂T ∈ D_m(U) (M_W(∂T) < ∞ for W ⊂⊂ U), there is a Borel measure ν with IsMassMeasure ∂T ν: ν(ℝ^P∖U) = 0 and ν(W) = M_W(∂T) < ∞ for open W ⊂⊂ U. By the definition of mass (applied to ±ψ/sup|ψ|), |∂T(ψ)| ≤ sup|ψ| · M_W(∂T) whenever ψ ∈ D^{n−1}(U) has tsupport ψ ⊆ W.

2. Good points (printed (2), (3), (10)). Let G be the set of x ∈ M such that
 (a) M has an approximate tangent space L_x with respect to θ at x (Definition 1.7 of Ch. 3: dim L_x = n and lim_{r↓0} ∫_{η_{x,r}(M)} f(y) θ(x + r y) dHⁿ(y) = θ(x) ∫_{L_x} f dHⁿ for all f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P), η_{x,r}(y) = (y − x)/r);
 (b) |ξ(x)| = 1;
 (c) μ(B̄_r(x)) > 0 for all r > 0 and lim_{r↓0} μ(B̄_r(x))^{-1} ∫_{B̄_r(x)} |ξ − ξ(x)| dμ = 0;
 (d) Θ*ⁿ(μ, x) < ∞;
 (e) Θ*ⁿ(ν, x) < ∞.
 Then Hⁿ(M∖G) = 0. (a) holds Hⁿ-a.e. on M by the sibling weighted_tangent_ae (its hypotheses are among ours). (b) holds by hypothesis. (c): for each q, μ⌞W_q is a finite Borel measure on ℝ^P and ξ ∈ L¹(μ⌞W_q) (it is bounded and measurable), so by the Besicovitch differentiation theorem (Simon Ch. 1, 3.23 with Remark 3.25(1): every Radon measure on ℝ^P has the symmetric Vitali property; Mathlib Besicovitch.vitaliFamily with VitaliFamily.ae_tendsto_average_norm_sub, the operator norm on Λ_n(ℝ^P) being equivalent to |·|) the statement (c) with μ⌞W_q in place of μ holds for μ⌞W_q-a.e. x; for x ∈ W_q and r < dist(x, ℝ^P∖W_q) the measures μ and μ⌞W_q agree on subsets of B̄_r(x), so (c) holds μ-a.e. on W_q, hence μ-a.e., hence Hⁿ-a.e. on M because Hⁿ⌞M ≪ μ. (d): for each q and t > 0, the sibling density_comparison with V := W_q and A := {x ∈ W_q : Θ*ⁿ(μ, x) ≥ t} gives t Hⁿ(A) ≤ μ(W_q) < ∞; letting t → ∞, Hⁿ({x ∈ W_q : Θ*ⁿ(μ, x) = ∞}) = 0, and we take the union over q (printed (2)). (e): the same argument with ν, ν(W_q) = M_{W_q}(∂T) < ∞ (printed (3)).
 Fix x ∈ G and write L := L_x. By (d), (e) there are C, r₀ > 0 with B̄_{r₀}(x) ⊆ U, μ(B̄_r(x)) ≤ C rⁿ and ν(B̄_r(x)) ≤ C rⁿ for 0 < r < r₀.

3. Blow-up of T (printed (11), (13)). For λ > 0 let η_λ(y) := (y − x)/λ. For ω ∈ Dⁿ(ℝ^P) with spt ω ⊆ B_R(0) let η_λ^#ω be the pulled-back form, (η_λ^#ω)(y) = λ^{-n} ω((y − x)/λ) (since Dη_λ = λ^{-1} Id). For 0 < λ < r₀/R it is smooth with support in B̄_{λR}(x) ⊆ U, so η_λ^#ω ∈ Dⁿ(U), and the change of variables y = x + λz (the similarity z ↦ x + λz maps η_λ(M) onto M and multiplies Hⁿ by λⁿ) gives
 T(η_λ^#ω) = ∫_M θ(y) λ^{-n} ⟨ω((y − x)/λ), ξ(y)⟩ dHⁿ(y) = ∫_{η_λ(M)} θ(x + λz) ⟨ω(z), ξ(x + λz)⟩ dHⁿ(z) = ∫_{η_λ(M)} f(z) θ(x + λz) dHⁿ(z) + e(λ),
 where f(z) := ⟨ω(z), ξ(x)⟩ is continuous with compact support and
 |e(λ)| ≤ sup|ω| ∫_{η_λ(M) ∩ B_R(0)} θ(x + λz) |ξ(x + λz) − ξ(x)| dHⁿ(z) = sup|ω| λ^{-n} ∫_{B_{λR}(x)} |ξ − ξ(x)| dμ ≤ sup|ω| · C Rⁿ · μ(B̄_{λR}(x))^{-1} ∫_{B̄_{λR}(x)} |ξ − ξ(x)| dμ → 0
 by (c) and (d). By (a), ∫_{η_λ(M)} f(z) θ(x + λz) dHⁿ(z) → θ(x) ∫_L f dHⁿ. Hence, for every ω ∈ Dⁿ(ℝ^P),
 lim_{λ↓0} T(η_λ^#ω) = S_x(ω) := θ(x) ∫_L ⟨ω(z), ξ(x)⟩ dHⁿ(z).

4. Boundary of the blow-up (printed (12)). Let φ ∈ D^{n−1}(ℝ^P) with spt φ ⊆ B_R(0). Then dφ ∈ Dⁿ(ℝ^P), spt dφ ⊆ B_R(0), and η_λ^#(dφ) = d(η_λ^#φ), so T(η_λ^#dφ) = T(d(η_λ^#φ)) = ∂T(η_λ^#φ). For 0 < λ < r₀/(2R), η_λ^#φ ∈ D^{n−1}(U) has tsupport in the ball W_λ := B_{2λR}(x), which is open with closure B̄_{2λR}(x) ⊆ U compact, i.e. W_λ ⊂⊂ U; and |(η_λ^#φ)(y)| = λ^{−(n−1)} |φ((y − x)/λ)| ≤ λ^{1−n} sup|φ|. By step 1 and IsMassMeasure ∂T ν,
 |T(η_λ^#dφ)| ≤ λ^{1−n} sup|φ| · M_{W_λ}(∂T) = λ^{1−n} sup|φ| · ν(W_λ) ≤ λ^{1−n} sup|φ| · C (2λR)ⁿ → 0 (λ ↓ 0).
 Hence S_x(dφ) = lim_{λ↓0} T(η_λ^#dφ) = 0 for every φ ∈ D^{n−1}(ℝ^P), i.e. ∂S_x = 0.

5. Orientation (printed argument after (13)). Choose an orthonormal basis τ₁, …, τ_P of ℝ^P such that τ₁, …, τ_n is an orthonormal basis of L (dim L = n ≤ P). Let y^j(z) := ⟨z, τ_j⟩, let dy^j be the corresponding constant 1-covectors, and for increasing J = (j₁ < ⋯ < j_n) let dy^J := dy^{j₁}∧⋯∧dy^{j_n} and τ_J := (τ_{j₁}, …, τ_{j_n}). Then dy^J(τ_K) = δ_{JK} for increasing J, K, every n-covector satisfies φ = Σ_J φ(τ_J) dy^J, and by the Cauchy-Binet formula (the change of basis is orthogonal) the dy^J are orthonormal for the Euclidean inner product on n-covectors, so |w|² = Σ_J w(dy^J)² for every n-vector w. subproblem.title: Sets with null rotated coordinate projections are null for the mass measure (Simon 6, Remark 2.35, Lemma 2.36, Remark 2.37(2))
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, n := m + 1, U ⊆ ℝ^P open, T ∈ D_n(U) with M_W(T) + M_W(∂T) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U, and μ a Borel measure on ℝ^P with IsMassMeasure T μ. Let Q be a linear isometry of ℝ^P and E ⊆ ℝ^P a Borel set such that Lⁿ(p_α(Q(E))) = 0 for every α ∈ I(n,P), where p_α : ℝ^P → ℝⁿ, x ↦ (x^{α(1)}, …, x^{α(n)}), and Lⁿ is Lebesgue measure (volume) on ℝⁿ. Then μ(E) = 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)), IsOpen U → ∀ T : GeometricCurrentOn U (m + 1), (∀ W, CompactlyContainedOpen W U → T.massOn W + T.boundary.massOn W < ∞) → ∀ μ : Measure (Eucl P), IsMassMeasure T μ → ∀ (Q : Eucl P ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] Eucl P) (E : Set (Eucl P)), MeasurableSet E → (∀ α : SimonMultiIndex (m + 1) P, (volume : Measure (Eucl (m + 1))) ((fun x : Eucl P => (WithLp.toLp 2 (fun i : Fin (m + 1) => Q x (α i)) : Eucl (m + 1))) '' E) = 0) → μ E = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Lemma 2.36 with its printed proof (displays (1)-(4)), Remark 2.37(2) and the inner-regularity step of Remark 2.37(1) (pp. 143-145). Following 2.37(2), the printed proof is run for Q_#T and read back on ℝ^P: π_α := p_α∘Q replaces p_α, and Q^*dx^α = π_α^*dy. It is given first for compact K (the printed step 'letting K be an arbitrary compact subset of E') and then extended to Borel E by inner regularity. The currents p_{α#}(T⌞ω_α) of the printed proof are realized as explicit linear functionals Y_α, so no general push-forward or restriction machinery is needed.

One input is proved differently. The printed proof takes from Remark 2.35 that the top-dimensional current p_{α#}(T⌞ω_α), which has finite mass and finite boundary mass, is given by a BV density. The only consequence it uses is that this current does not charge Lⁿ-null sets. Remark 2.35 rests on the compactness theorem for BV functions (Simon Ch. 2, 2.6), which the pinned library lacks: SimonGMT Chapter02/BV.lean only proves closure statements for sequences that already converge. Step 3 therefore replaces 2.35 by a self-contained quantitative estimate. It uses the Newtonian-potential representation of a compactly supported smooth function (D. Gilbarg and N. S. Trudinger, Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order, Lemma 7.14). Step 4 turns it into the bound |Y_α(a)| ≤ C_α sup|a|·Lⁿ(spt a)^{1/n}, which is what display (2) of the printed proof needs.

Erratum: in 2.37(2) the printed implication 'Lⁿ(Q(E)) = 0 for each α ⇒ μ_T(E) = 0' should read 'Lⁿ(p_α(Q(E))) = 0 for each α ⇒ μ_T(E) = 0'.

1. Notation and the degenerate case. Throughout, n = m + 1. |·| is the Euclidean coefficient norm on covectors and multivectors (Simon 6, Remark 2.6; covectorEuclideanNorm), and I := I(n,P).
 For J = (j₁ < ⋯ < j_r) ⊆ {1, …, P} write dx^J := dx^{j₁}∧⋯∧dx^{j_r}, and let Q^*dx^J denote its pull-back by Q.
 π_α := p_α∘Q : ℝ^P → ℝⁿ is linear. On ℝⁿ use coordinates y¹, …, yⁿ, and write dy := dy¹∧⋯∧dyⁿ and dy^{(ĵ)} := dy¹∧⋯∧dy^{j−1}∧dy^{j+1}∧⋯∧dyⁿ. Then π_α^*dy^i = Q^*dx^{α(i)}, π_α^*dy = Q^*dx^α and π_α^*dy^{(ĵ)} = Q^*dx^{α_ĵ}, where α_ĵ ∈ I(n−1,P) is α with its j-th entry removed.
 By the Cauchy-Binet formula, for r = n and for r = n − 1 the covectors Q^*dx^J (J ∈ I(r,P)) form an orthonormal basis of the r-covectors for the Euclidean inner product: their Gram matrix (det((QQ^T)_{JJ′}))_{J,J′} is the identity.
 Constants: ω_n := Lⁿ(B_1(0)), and c_n is a constant with |γ∧φ| ≤ c_n|γ||φ| for all 1-covectors γ and (n−1)-covectors φ on ℝ^P (the wedge product is bilinear on finite-dimensional spaces; in fact c_n = 1 works).
 If P < n, then I = ∅, every n-covector on ℝ^P is 0, every ω ∈ Dⁿ(U) is 0, T = 0 and M_W(T) = 0. Hence μ(W) = 0 for every open W ⊂⊂ U and μ(ℝ^P∖U) = 0. Since U is a countable union of open W ⊂⊂ U, μ = 0 and the claim holds. Assume P ≥ n from now on.

2. Representation and mass bounds. Apply the sibling mass_measure_representation to T, whose local masses are finite. It gives a strongly measurable ξ : ℝ^P → Λ_n(ℝ^P) with |ξ| = 1 μ-a.e. such that T(ω) = ∫⟨ω, ξ⟩dμ for every ω ∈ Dⁿ(U), with μ-integrable integrand. Also μ(W) = M_W(T) < ∞ for open W ⊂⊂ U.
 M_W is the supremum of T(φ) over φ with tsupport φ ⊆ W and |φ| ≤ 1 (SimonGMT massOn, massAdmissibleOn). Applying the definition to ±φ/sup|φ| gives the mass bounds: |T(φ)| ≤ sup|φ|·M_W(T) and |∂T(ψ)| ≤ sup|ψ|·M_W(∂T) whenever φ ∈ Dⁿ(U) and ψ ∈ D^{n−1}(U) have tsupport in the open set W ⊂⊂ U.

3. A potential estimate (replaces Remark 2.35). For w ∈ ℝⁿ∖{0} and j = 1, …, n put K_j(w) := w_j/(nω_n|w|ⁿ), and K_j(0) := 0.
 Claim: let a ∈ C_c^∞(ℝⁿ) and ψ_j := K_j * a, i.e. ψ_j(y) = ∫K_j(y − z)a(z)dz. Then each ψ_j is C^∞ on ℝⁿ, Σ_{j=1}^n ∂_jψ_j = a, and sup_{ℝⁿ}|ψ_j| ≤ ((n+1)/n)·sup|a|·(Lⁿ(spt a)/ω_n)^{1/n} for every j.
 Proof. (i) We have |K_j(w)| ≤ |w|^{1−n}/(nω_n). By polar coordinates, ∫_{B_ρ(0)}|w|^{1−n}dw = nω_nρ (Mathlib Measure.measurePreserving_homeomorphUnitSphereProd; the surface measure of S^{n−1} is nω_n by Measure.toSphere_apply_univ). So K_j ∈ L¹_loc(ℝⁿ). Being the convolution of a locally integrable function with a compactly supported smooth function, ψ_j = K_j * a is C^∞, and ∂^βψ_j = K_j * ∂^βa for every multi-index β (Mathlib HasCompactSupport.contDiff_convolution_right, HasCompactSupport.hasFDerivAt_convolution_right).
 (ii) Fix y ∈ ℝⁿ. For every unit vector θ, since a has compact support, a(y) = −∫_0^∞(d/dt)a(y + tθ)dt = −∫_0^∞∇a(y + tθ)·θ dt. Integrate over θ ∈ S^{n−1} with respect to the surface measure σ, where σ(S^{n−1}) = nω_n. Then use polar coordinates about y: ∫_{ℝⁿ}g(z)dz = ∫_{S^{n−1}}∫_0^∞g(y + tθ)t^{n−1}dt dσ(θ), with g(z) := ∇a(z)·(z − y)/|z − y|ⁿ. For this g, g(y + tθ)t^{n−1} = ∇a(y + tθ)·θ, and g is integrable because |g(z)| ≤ sup|∇a|·1_{spt a}(z)·|z − y|^{1−n}. This gives nω_n·a(y) = −∫∇a(z)·(z − y)|z − y|^{−n}dz. Equivalently, a(y) = Σ_j∫K_j(y − z)∂_ja(z)dz = Σ_j(K_j * ∂_ja)(y), which equals Σ_j∂_jψ_j(y) by (i). For n = 1, S⁰ = {±1} carries counting measure, nω_n = 2, and this is the fundamental theorem of calculus.
 (iii) Let S := spt a. If Lⁿ(S) = 0, then the open set {a ≠ 0} ⊆ S is Lⁿ-null, hence empty, so a ≡ 0, ψ_j ≡ 0 and the claim is trivial. Otherwise let ρ := (Lⁿ(S)/ω_n)^{1/n} > 0. Then |ψ_j(y)| ≤ sup|a|·(nω_n)^{−1}∫_S|y − z|^{1−n}dz. Moreover ∫_S|y − z|^{1−n}dz ≤ ∫_{B_ρ(y)}|y − z|^{1−n}dz + ∫_{S∖B_ρ(y)}ρ^{1−n}dz ≤ nω_nρ + ρ^{1−n}Lⁿ(S) = (n + 1)ω_nρ. Hence |ψ_j(y)| ≤ ((n+1)/n)·sup|a|·ρ. ∎

4. The functionals Y_α (printed (1)) and their potential bound. Fix an open W ⊂⊂ U and ω ∈ Dⁿ(U) with tsupport ω ⊆ W and |ω| ≤ 1.
 Write ω = Σ_{α∈I}ω_αQ^*dx^α with ω_α := ⟨ω, Q^*dx^α⟩ (the orthonormal expansion of step 1). Then ω_α ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^P), tsupport ω_α ⊆ W, |ω_α| ≤ |ω| ≤ 1, and T(ω) = Σ_αT(ω_αQ^*dx^α).
 Fix α and write π := π_α. For a ∈ C^∞(ℝⁿ) set Y_α(a) := T(ω_α·(a∘π)·Q^*dx^α). The form is smooth with tsupport in tsupport ω_α ⊆ W, so it lies in Dⁿ(U). (Y_α(a) is Simon's p_{α#}(T⌞ω_α)(a dy), written for Q_#T.) By step 2, Y_α(a) = ∫ω_α(x)a(π(x))⟨Q^*dx^α, ξ(x)⟩dμ(x).
 Claim: for every a ∈ C_c^∞(ℝⁿ), |Y_α(a)| ≤ C_α·sup|a|·Lⁿ(spt a)^{1/n}, where C_α := (n + 1)ω_n^{−1/n}(M_W(∂T)·sup|ω_α| + c_nM_W(T)·sup|dω_α|).
 Proof. Take the ψ_j of step 3 and the smooth (n−1)-form ψ̂ := Σ_j(−1)^{j−1}ψ_j dy^{(ĵ)} on ℝⁿ; then dψ̂ = (Σ_j∂_jψ_j)dy = a dy. Its pull-back π^#ψ̂ = Σ_j(−1)^{j−1}(ψ_j∘π)Q^*dx^{α_ĵ} is smooth on ℝ^P, and d(π^#ψ̂) = π^#(dψ̂) = (a∘π)Q^*dx^α.
 Put Φ := ω_απ^#ψ̂ ∈ D^{n−1}(U); its tsupport lies in tsupport ω_α ⊆ W. Then dΦ = dω_α∧π^#ψ̂ + ω_α(a∘π)Q^*dx^α, so
 Y_α(a) = T(dΦ) − T(dω_α∧π^#ψ̂) = ∂T(Φ) − T(dω_α∧π^#ψ̂).
 The (n−1)-covectors Q^*dx^{α_ĵ} (j = 1, …, n) are orthonormal (step 1). So by step 3, |π^#ψ̂(x)| = (Σ_jψ_j(πx)²)^{1/2} ≤ n·max_jsup|ψ_j| ≤ (n + 1)ω_n^{−1/n}·sup|a|·Lⁿ(spt a)^{1/n}.
 Both forms have tsupport in W, so the mass bounds of step 2 give |∂T(Φ)| ≤ M_W(∂T)·sup|ω_α|·sup|π^#ψ̂| and |T(dω_α∧π^#ψ̂)| ≤ M_W(T)·c_n·sup|dω_α|·sup|π^#ψ̂|. Adding the two bounds proves the claim. ∎

5. Printed (2)-(4) for compact K. Let K ⊆ U be compact with Lⁿ(π_α(K)) = 0 for every α ∈ I. Fix W, ω and α as in step 4, and let F := π_α(K), a compact Lⁿ-null set.
 For ε > 0 let G_ε := {y ∈ ℝⁿ : dist(y, F) < ε}. The G_ε are open, decrease as ε ↓ 0, and intersect to F. By continuity from above (Lⁿ(G_1) < ∞), Lⁿ(G_ε) → Lⁿ(F) = 0.
 Let φ_ε be a mollifier supported in B_{ε/4}(0), and set b_ε := 1_{G_{ε/2}} * φ_ε. Then b_ε ∈ C_c^∞(ℝⁿ), 0 ≤ b_ε ≤ 1, b_ε = 1 on G_{ε/4} (a neighbourhood of F), and spt b_ε ⊆ G_ε. Fix χ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝⁿ) with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1 and χ = 1 on a neighbourhood of the compact set π_α(tsupport ω_α). Then ω_α·(χ∘π_α) = ω_α, so
 T(ω_αQ^*dx^α) = Y_α(χ) = Y_α(b_εχ) + Y_α((1 − b_ε)χ).
 First term: sup|b_εχ| ≤ 1 and spt(b_εχ) ⊆ G_ε, so step 4 gives |Y_α(b_εχ)| ≤ C_α·Lⁿ(G_ε)^{1/n}.
 Second term: by the integral formula of step 4, Y_α((1 − b_ε)χ) = ∫ω_α(x)(1 − b_ε(π_αx))⟨Q^*dx^α, ξ(x)⟩dμ(x). The integrand vanishes outside tsupport ω_α ⊆ W and on K, where b_ε∘π_α = 1. It is bounded by 1 μ-a.e., because |ω_α| ≤ 1, 0 ≤ 1 − b_ε ≤ 1 and |⟨Q^*dx^α, ξ⟩| ≤ |Q^*dx^α||ξ| = 1. Hence |Y_α((1 − b_ε)χ)| ≤ μ(W∖K).
 Letting ε ↓ 0 gives |T(ω_αQ^*dx^α)| ≤ μ(W∖K). Summing over α gives T(ω) ≤ N·μ(W∖K) with N := #I. Taking the supremum over admissible ω, M_W(T) ≤ N·μ(W∖K) (printed (3)), i.e. μ(W) ≤ N·μ(W∖K) for every open W ⊂⊂ U (printed (4)).
 Now choose r₀ > 0 with {x : dist(x, K) ≤ r₀} ⊆ U (possible since K is compact and U open; any r₀ works if U = ℝ^P), and put W_q := {x : dist(x, K) < r₀/q}. The W_q are open, ⊂⊂ U and decreasing, with ⋂_qW_q = K. Since μ(W₁) < ∞, continuity from above gives μ(W_q∖K) → μ(∅) = 0. Hence μ(K) ≤ μ(W_q) ≤ N·μ(W_q∖K) → 0, i.e. μ(K) = 0.

6. Borel E (inner regularity, 1.15 of Ch. 1, as in 2.37(1)). Let E be Borel with Lⁿ(p_α(Q(E))) = Lⁿ(π_α(E)) = 0 for all α. Since μ(ℝ^P∖U) = 0, μ(E) = μ(E ∩ U).
 Let (W_q) be open sets ⊂⊂ U with U = ⋃_qW_q. Each μ⌞W_q is a finite Borel measure on the metric space ℝ^P, so by Simon Ch. 1, 1.15(2), μ(E ∩ W_q) = sup{μ(C) : C ⊆ E ∩ W_q closed}.
 Every such C lies in the compact set closure(W_q) ⊆ U, so it is a compact subset of U, and π_α(C) ⊆ π_α(E) is Lⁿ-null for every α. Hence μ(C) = 0 by step 5. Thus μ(E ∩ W_q) = 0 for all q, and μ(E) ≤ Σ_qμ(E ∩ W_q) = 0. ∎

subproblem.title: Besicovitch-Federer projection theorem for almost every linear map (finite measure)
subproblem.statement: Let N, m ∈ ℕ, k := m + 1, and let E ⊆ ℝ^N be a Borel set with Hᵏ(E) < ∞ (Hᵏ = μHE[k]) which is purely k-unrectifiable. Then for Lebesgue-almost every v = (v₁, …, v_k) ∈ (ℝ^N)^k, the image of E under the linear map L_v : ℝ^N → ℝᵏ, x ↦ (⟨v₁,x⟩, …, ⟨v_k,x⟩), has Lebesgue measure zero in ℝᵏ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N m : ℕ) (E : Set (Eucl N)), MeasurableSet E → (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl N)) E < ∞ → Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter03.PurelyUnrectifiable (m + 1) E → ∀ᵐ v ∂(volume : Measure (Fin (m + 1) → Eucl N)), (volume : Measure (Eucl (m + 1))) ((fun x : Eucl N => (WithLp.toLp 2 (fun i : Fin (m + 1) => inner ℝ (v i) x) : Eucl (m + 1))) '' E) = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: P. Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces, Theorem 18.1: the Besicovitch-Federer projection theorem, direction 'purely unrectifiable ⇒ almost all projections null'. We follow the proof of Theorem 1.2 ('only if' part) in R. Hovila, E. Järvenpää, M. Järvenpää and F. Ledrappier, Geom. Dedicata 161 (2012), arXiv:1104.3453, which combines its Lemmas 2.2-2.4. Here it is applied to the family of linear maps L_v, v ∈ (ℝ^N)^k (the k×N matrices with rows v₁, …, v_k). Simon states the projection theorem as Ch. 3, 3.6 without proof ([Fed69, 3.3.13]).
 The ingredients are: the sibling bf_cone_density (Lemma 2.2 there: E_{1,δ} is null); the sibling bf_trichotomy (Lemma 2.4 there); the sibling density_comparison (first part of Lemma 2.3 there: E_{2,δ} has null image); and Eilenberg's inequality (second part of Lemma 2.3 there; Simon Ch. 2, 1.8(ii)), which is proved in step 3(c).

Notation: k := m + 1, Hᵏ := μHE[k], L_v(x) := (⟨v₁,x⟩, …, ⟨v_k,x⟩), and ‖L_v‖ is its operator norm. Lᵏ := volume on ℝᵏ, which equals Hᵏ = μHE[k] on ℝᵏ (Mathlib InnerProductSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume; kernel-checked as v2_glue_volume). ℒ := volume on (ℝ^N)^k, the product of the Lebesgue measures. For any S ⊆ ℝ^N and every v, Hᵏ(L_v(S)) ≤ ‖L_v‖ᵏHᵏ(S) (Lipschitz image bound; SimonGMT euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image_le_of_lipschitzOn).

1. Reduction to σ-compact E. μ_E := Hᵏ⌞E is a finite Borel measure on ℝ^N, hence inner regular. So there are compact K₁ ⊆ K₂ ⊆ ⋯ ⊆ E with Hᵏ(E∖⋃_iK_i) = 0. Put E′ := ⋃_iK_i. It is σ-compact and Borel, Hᵏ(E′) < ∞, and E′ is purely k-unrectifiable as a subset of E. For every v, Lᵏ(L_v(E)) ≤ Lᵏ(L_v(E′)) + ‖L_v‖ᵏHᵏ(E∖E′) = Lᵏ(L_v(E′)). So it suffices to treat E′; from now on write E for E′, which is σ-compact.

2. A full-measure set of v. For l ∈ ℕ put δ_l := 1/(l + 1). By the sibling bf_trichotomy with δ := δ_l, there are ℒ-null sets 𝒩_l such that for v ∉ 𝒩_l and Hᵏ-a.e. a ∈ E, at least one of (T1)_l, (T2), (T3)_l holds, where:
 (T1)_l: for every η > 0 there is s ∈ (0,1) with Hᵏ(E ∩ X_v(a,r,s)) ≤ η(rs)ᵏ for all r ∈ (0,δ_l);
 (T2): dimensionalUpperDensity ν_v k univ (L_va) = ∞, with ν_v := (L_v)_#(Hᵏ⌞E);
 (T3)_l: some x ∈ E with x ≠ a and |x − a| < δ_l has L_vx = L_va.
 Let 𝒩 := ⋃_l𝒩_l, an ℒ-null set, and fix v ∉ 𝒩. Taking the countable union of the exceptional null sets, there is Z ⊆ E with Hᵏ(Z) = 0 such that every a ∈ E∖Z satisfies, for every l, (T1)_l or (T2) or (T3)_l.

3. Splitting E. Let E₁^{(l)} := {a ∈ E : (T1)_l}, E₂ := {a ∈ E : (T2)} and E₃ := {a ∈ E : (T3)_l holds for every l}. If a ∈ E∖Z lies neither in E₂ nor in E₃, then (T3)_l fails for some l, so a ∈ E₁^{(l)}. Hence E ⊆ Z ∪ ⋃_lE₁^{(l)} ∪ E₂ ∪ E₃, and L_v(E) ⊆ L_v(Z) ∪ ⋃_lL_v(E₁^{(l)}) ∪ L_v(E₂) ∪ L_v(E₃).
 (a) E₁^{(l)} is exactly the set E₁ of the sibling bf_cone_density for this E, this v and δ := δ_l; its hypotheses hold because E is purely k-unrectifiable. So Hᵏ(E₁^{(l)}) = 0 and Lᵏ(L_v(E₁^{(l)})) ≤ ‖L_v‖ᵏ·0 = 0. Likewise Lᵏ(L_v(Z)) = 0.
 (b) L_v(E₂) ⊆ Y := {y ∈ ℝᵏ : dimensionalUpperDensity ν_v k univ y = ∞}. Apply the sibling density_comparison in ℝᵏ with ν := ν_v, A := Y, V := ℝᵏ and t := ∞. It gives ∞·Hᵏ(Y) ≤ ν_v(ℝᵏ) = Hᵏ(E) < ∞, so Hᵏ(Y) = 0, i.e. Lᵏ(Y) = 0 (kernel-checked as v2_glue_infinite_density).
 (c) Eilenberg's inequality. If a ∈ E₃, the fibre E ∩ L_v^{−1}(L_va) contains, for every l, a point x ≠ a with |x − a| < δ_l, so it is infinite. Hence L_v(E₃) ⊆ Y₃ := {y : #(E ∩ L_v^{−1}(y)) = ∞}.
 For i ∈ ℕ let 𝒬_i be the partition of ℝ^N into half-open dyadic cubes of side 2^{−i}, and let N_i(y) := #{Q ∈ 𝒬_i : y ∈ L_v(E ∩ Q)}. A half-open cube is a countable union of closed cubes, so each E ∩ Q is σ-compact; hence L_v(E ∩ Q) is σ-compact and Borel, and N_i is Borel.
 Each cube of 𝒬_{i+1} lies in exactly one cube of 𝒬_i, so N_i ≤ N_{i+1}. Moreover N_i(y) ↑ #(E ∩ L_v^{−1}(y)) as i → ∞, because finitely many distinct points of the fibre lie in distinct cubes of 𝒬_i once √N·2^{−i} is smaller than their minimal distance.
 By monotone convergence, the Lipschitz image bound, and additivity of Hᵏ on the Borel partition {E ∩ Q : Q ∈ 𝒬_i} of E,
 ∫#(E ∩ L_v^{−1}(y))dLᵏ(y) = lim_iΣ_{Q∈𝒬_i}Lᵏ(L_v(E ∩ Q)) ≤ lim_iΣ_{Q∈𝒬_i}‖L_v‖ᵏHᵏ(E ∩ Q) = ‖L_v‖ᵏHᵏ(E) < ∞.
 Hence Lᵏ(Y₃) = 0, and so Lᵏ(L_v(E₃)) = 0.
 Therefore Lᵏ(L_v(E)) = 0 for every v ∉ 𝒩, i.e. for ℒ-a.e. v. ∎
proof_key_steps: Reduce to σ-compact E by inner regularity; the remaining null part has a null image under every Lipschitz map L_v.
Apply bf_trichotomy with δ = 1/(l+1) for every l: for a.e. v, a.e. a ∈ E satisfies, for each l, (T1)_l, (T2) or (T3)_l.
Points satisfying some (T1)_l form Hᵏ-null sets by bf_cone_density, so their images are null.
Points satisfying (T2) map into the infinite-density set of the finite measure (L_v)_#(Hᵏ⌞E), which is null by density_comparison.
Points satisfying (T3)_l for all l have infinite fibres, whose images are null by Eilenberg's inequality (dyadic cubes and monotone convergence).
Hence Lᵏ(L_v(E)) = 0 for a.e. v.

subproblem.title: Absolute continuity of the mass measure with respect to Hⁿ (Simon 6, Remark 2.37(1))
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, n := m + 1, U ⊆ ℝ^P open, T ∈ D_n(U) with M_W(T) + M_W(∂T) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U, and μ a Borel measure on ℝ^P with IsMassMeasure T μ. Then μ is absolutely continuous with respect to n-dimensional Hausdorff measure Hⁿ = μHE[n] on ℝ^P: every set A ⊆ ℝ^P with Hⁿ(A) = 0 has μ(A) = 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)), IsOpen U → ∀ T : GeometricCurrentOn U (m + 1), (∀ W, CompactlyContainedOpen W U → T.massOn W + T.boundary.massOn W < ∞) → ∀ μ : Measure (Eucl P), IsMassMeasure T μ → μ ≪ (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P))
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, Remark 2.37(1) (p. 144): ‘The hypothesis Lⁿ(p_α(E)) = 0 is trivially satisfied if Hⁿ(E) = 0 … hence the lemma implies that if C is a Borel set with Hⁿ(C) = 0 then μ_T(C) = 0. That is, μ_T is absolutely continuous with respect to Hⁿ in U provided M_W(T), M_W(∂T) < ∞ ∀ W ⊂⊂ U.’ The inner-regularity step of the printed remark is already contained in the sibling projection_null, which is stated for Borel sets and a rotation Q (here Q is the identity).

1. Let A ⊆ ℝ^P with Hⁿ(A) = 0. Since Hⁿ is Borel regular (the outer measure of a measure is attained on a measurable hull), there is a Borel set B ⊇ A with Hⁿ(B) = 0, e.g. B := toMeasurable Hⁿ A. As μ(A) ≤ μ(B), it suffices to show μ(B) = 0.

2. For α ∈ I(n,P) the coordinate projection p_α : ℝ^P → ℝⁿ, x ↦ (x^{α(1)}, …, x^{α(n)}), is 1-Lipschitz: |p_α(x) − p_α(y)|² = Σ_i (x − y)_{α(i)}² ≤ |x − y|², because α is injective. A map that is Lipschitz with constant 1 does not increase n-dimensional Hausdorff measure (Mathlib LipschitzWith.hausdorffMeasure_image_le; μHE[n] is the fixed positive multiple addHaarScalarFactor(volume, μH[n])·μH[n] on every metric space), so Hⁿ(p_α(B)) ≤ Hⁿ(B) = 0. On ℝⁿ, Hⁿ = μHE[n] equals Lebesgue measure Lⁿ (Simon Ch. 1, 2.8-2.10; Mathlib InnerProductSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume). Hence Lⁿ(p_α(B)) = 0 for every α.

3. Apply the sibling projection_null to T, μ, the identity isometry Q := id of ℝ^P and the Borel set E := B: its hypothesis Lⁿ(p_α(Q(B))) = Lⁿ(p_α(B)) = 0 holds for every α by step 2 (if P < n there is no α and the hypothesis is vacuous). Therefore μ(B) = 0.

4. Hence μ(A) = 0 for every Hⁿ-null A ⊆ ℝ^P, i.e. μ ≪ Hⁿ. ∎
proof_key_steps: Replace the Hⁿ-null set A by a Borel Hⁿ-null hull B ⊇ A.
Coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz, so Lⁿ(p_α(B)) = Hⁿ(p_α(B)) ≤ Hⁿ(B) = 0 for all α.
projection_null with Q = id and E = B gives μ(B) = 0, hence μ(A) = 0.

audit.reason: The measurable hull, coordinate-projection Lipschitz bound and normalized Hausdorff/Lebesgue identity justify applying projection_null with the identity isometry. This proves absolute continuity for arbitrary null sets; the reduction also passes Lean checking.

subproblem.title: A rotation making all coordinate projections of a purely unrectifiable set null (Simon 3, Structure Theorem 3.6, as used in 8.1)
subproblem.statement: For P, m ∈ ℕ and n := m + 1, let A ⊆ ℝ^P be purely n-unrectifiable (every countably n-rectifiable subset of A has Hⁿ-measure 0) and Hⁿ-σ-finite (A ⊆ ⋃_{j∈ℕ} S_j with Hⁿ(S_j) < ∞ for all j). Then there is a linear isometry Q of ℝ^P such that Lⁿ(p_α(Q(A))) = 0 for every α ∈ I(n,P), where p_α(x) = (x^{α(1)}, …, x^{α(n)}) and Lⁿ is Lebesgue measure on ℝⁿ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (A : Set (Eucl P)), Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter03.PurelyUnrectifiable (m + 1) A → (∃ S : ℕ → Set (Eucl P), A ⊆ ⋃ j, S j ∧ ∀ j, (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P)) (S j) < ∞) → ∃ Q : Eucl P ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] Eucl P, ∀ α : SimonMultiIndex (m + 1) P, (volume : Measure (Eucl (m + 1))) ((fun x : Eucl P => (WithLp.toLp 2 (fun i : Fin (m + 1) => Q x (α i)) : Eucl (m + 1))) '' A) = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, proof of 8.1 (p. 174): 'By the Structure Theorem 3.6 of Ch. 3 we have an orthogonal transformation Q of ℝ^{n+ℓ} such that Hⁿ(p_α(QP)) = 0 for each α = (i₁, …, i_n) with 1 ≤ i₁ < i₂ < ⋯ < i_n ≤ n+ℓ'. Simon, Ch. 3, Theorem 3.6 (p. 80) states the projection theorem without proof, referring to [Fed69, 3.3.13] and [Ros84]. Here the projection theorem is the sibling bf_projection_null_ae: the finite-measure Besicovitch-Federer theorem for almost every linear map ℝ^P → ℝⁿ, proved there in full through its siblings bf_cone_density, mickle_rado and bf_trichotomy (Mattila, Geometry of Sets and Measures in Euclidean Spaces, Ch. 18; Hovila-Järvenpää-Järvenpää-Ledrappier, arXiv:1104.3453, §2).
 This proof does two things. First, it reduces the σ-finite, possibly nonmeasurable set A to sets to which that sibling applies (step 2, as in Simon's Lemma 3.2). Second, it transfers 'almost every linear map' to 'some orthogonal Q' (steps 4-5), replacing the transport through the Grassmannian in Simon's formulation of 3.6 by Haar measure on O(P) realized through the Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization of a Gaussian matrix.
 Notation: n := m + 1, Hⁿ := μHE[n], and Lⁿ := volume on ℝⁿ (= Hⁿ there). For v = (v₁, …, v_n) ∈ (ℝ^P)^n, L_v(x) := (⟨v₁,x⟩, …, ⟨v_n,x⟩) with operator norm ‖L_v‖, and ℒ := volume on (ℝ^P)^n.

1. Case P < n. Then I(n,P) = ∅, since there is no strictly increasing map {1, …, n} → {1, …, P}. So Q := identity satisfies the conclusion vacuously. Assume P ≥ n from now on.

2. Reduction to σ-compact sets of finite measure. Let A_j := A ∩ S_j. Then A = ⋃_jA_j, Hⁿ(A_j) < ∞, and each A_j is purely n-unrectifiable (subsets of purely unrectifiable sets are purely unrectifiable).
 Choose a Borel set B_j ⊇ A_j with Hⁿ(B_j ∩ F) = Hⁿ(A_j ∩ F) for every Borel F; such a measurable hull exists because Hⁿ(A_j) < ∞ (Mathlib toMeasurable, Measure.measure_toMeasurable_inter). By Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3 in its Borel form (SimonGMT measurable_rectifiable_purelyUnrectifiable_decomposition), B_j = R_j ∪ P_j with R_j Borel and countably n-rectifiable and P_j purely n-unrectifiable. Then Hⁿ(R_j) = Hⁿ(R_j ∩ B_j) = Hⁿ(R_j ∩ A_j) = 0, since R_j ∩ A_j is a countably n-rectifiable subset of A.
 Consequently B_j is purely n-unrectifiable: for countably rectifiable S ⊆ B_j, Hⁿ(S) ≤ Hⁿ(S ∩ R_j) + Hⁿ(S ∩ P_j) = 0. Also Hⁿ(B_j) = Hⁿ(A_j) < ∞.
 Since Hⁿ⌞B_j is a finite Borel measure on ℝ^P, it is inner regular, so there is a σ-compact C_j ⊆ B_j with Hⁿ(B_j∖C_j) = 0. Each C_j is Borel, has Hⁿ(C_j) < ∞, and is purely n-unrectifiable.

3. Almost every linear map. By the sibling bf_projection_null_ae with N := P and E := C_j, ℒ({v : Lⁿ(L_v(C_j)) > 0}) = 0 for each j. Let Z := ⋃_j{v ∈ (ℝ^P)^n : Lⁿ(L_v(C_j)) > 0}.
 (a) ℒ(Z) = 0.
 (b) Z is Borel. First, for compact K the map v ↦ Lⁿ(L_v(K)) is upper semicontinuous. Indeed, let v_l → v and ε > 0. Since |L_{v_l}x − L_vx| ≤ ‖L_{v_l} − L_v‖·sup_K|x|, for large l the set L_{v_l}(K) lies in the open ε-neighbourhood U_ε of the compact set L_v(K). So limsup_lLⁿ(L_{v_l}(K)) ≤ Lⁿ(U_ε), and Lⁿ(U_ε) ↓ Lⁿ(L_v(K)) as ε ↓ 0. Now write C_j = ⋃_iK_{j,i} with K_{j,i} compact and increasing in i. Then Lⁿ(L_v(C_j)) = sup_iLⁿ(L_v(K_{j,i})) is Borel in v.
 (c) Z is invariant under GL(n). Let G be an invertible n×n matrix and Gv := (Σ_lG_{1l}v_l, …, Σ_lG_{nl}v_l). Then L_{Gv} = G∘L_v, so Lⁿ(L_{Gv}(C_j)) = |det G|·Lⁿ(L_v(C_j)) (Mathlib Measure.addHaar_image_linearMap). Hence v ∈ Z ⟺ Gv ∈ Z.
 (d) For v ∉ Z, Lⁿ(L_v(A)) = 0. Indeed A ⊆ ⋃_jB_j ⊆ ⋃_jC_j ∪ ⋃_j(B_j∖C_j). So, by the Lipschitz image bound and Lⁿ = Hⁿ on ℝⁿ, Lⁿ(L_v(A)) ≤ Σ_jLⁿ(L_v(C_j)) + Σ_j‖L_v‖ⁿHⁿ(B_j∖C_j) = 0.

4. Rows of an orthogonal matrix. Let O(P) be the group of orthogonal P×P matrices, i.e. the linear isometries of ℝ^P. For Q ∈ O(P) and α ∈ I(n,P) let Φ_α(Q) := (Q^Te_{α(1)}, …, Q^Te_{α(n)}) ∈ (ℝ^P)^n, the rows α(1), …, α(n) of Q. For x ∈ ℝ^P, p_α(Qx) = ((Qx)^{α(i)})_i = (⟨Q^Te_{α(i)}, x⟩)_i = L_{Φ_α(Q)}(x). So p_α∘Q = L_{Φ_α(Q)}; this was kernel-checked as v2_glue_rows, with Q^T = Q.symm. By step 3(d), it therefore suffices to find Q ∈ O(P) with Φ_α(Q) ∉ Z for every α ∈ I(n,P).

5. Haar measure. O(P) is a compact metrizable topological group; let h be its left-invariant Haar probability measure (Mathlib Measure.haarMeasure, normalized). We use two facts.
 (H1) h is invariant under left multiplication (by construction).
 (H2) Every right-invariant Borel probability measure ν on O(P) equals h. Proof, using only (H1) and Fubini: for Borel S, ν(S) = ∫_{O(P)}ν(Sg^{−1})dh(g) = ∫∫1_S(xg)dν(x)dh(g) = ∫∫1_S(xg)dh(g)dν(x) = ∫h(x^{−1}S)dν(x) = h(S).
 (a) A Gaussian construction of h. Let γ be the standard Gaussian probability measure on ℝ^{P×P}, with density (2π)^{−P²/2}exp(−Σ_{i,l}A_{il}²/2), and let A be a γ-distributed matrix with rows a₁, …, a_P. Almost surely A is invertible. By Fubini, given a₁, …, a_{i−1}, the row a_i lies in their span (a proper subspace, hence Lebesgue-null) with probability 0.
 Let GS(A) ∈ O(P) be the row Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization of A. Its rows are q₁ := a₁/|a₁| and q_i := (a_i − Σ_{l<i}⟨a_i,q_l⟩q_l)/|a_i − Σ_{l<i}⟨a_i,q_l⟩q_l|. GS is continuous on the invertible matrices; we set GS(A) := I on the null set of singular matrices, so that GS is Borel.
 For Q′ ∈ O(P), the rows of AQ′ are Q′^Ta_i, which have the same inner products as the a_i; hence GS(AQ′) = GS(A)Q′. Also γ is invariant under A ↦ AQ′: the density depends only on Σ_i|a_i|² = Σ_i|Q′^Ta_i|², and A ↦ AQ′ is a linear isometry of ℝ^{P×P}. Hence the law of GS(A) is a right-invariant Borel probability measure on O(P), and by (H2) it equals h.
 (b) h(Φ_{α₀}^{−1}(Z)) = 0 for α₀ := (1, …, n). The Gram-Schmidt process produces q₁, …, q_n from a₁, …, a_n alone. So the first n rows of GS(A) are (q₁, …, q_n) = T(a₁, …, a_n) for an invertible lower-triangular n×n matrix T depending on A. By 3(c), Φ_{α₀}(GS(A)) ∈ Z ⟺ (a₁, …, a_n) ∈ Z. Therefore h(Φ_{α₀}^{−1}(Z)) = P(Φ_{α₀}(GS(A)) ∈ Z) = P((a₁, …, a_n) ∈ Z) = 0. The last equality holds because (a₁, …, a_n) has a density on (ℝ^P)^n and ℒ(Z) = 0 by 3(a). (Φ_{α₀}^{−1}(Z) is Borel by 3(b) and the continuity of Φ_{α₀}.)
 (c) General α. Let σ be a permutation of {1, …, P} with σ(i) = α(i) for i ≤ n, and let Π ∈ O(P) be the permutation matrix with Π^Te_i = e_{σ(i)} for all i. Then Φ_{α₀}(ΠQ) = (Q^TΠ^Te_i)_{i≤n} = (Q^Te_{α(i)})_{i≤n} = Φ_α(Q). Hence Φ_α^{−1}(Z) = Π^{−1}Φ_{α₀}^{−1}(Z), and h(Φ_α^{−1}(Z)) = h(Φ_{α₀}^{−1}(Z)) = 0 by left invariance (H1).

6. Conclusion. The finite union ⋃_{α∈I(n,P)}Φ_α^{−1}(Z) has h-measure 0 < 1 = h(O(P)). So there is Q ∈ O(P) with Φ_α(Q) ∉ Z for every α. By steps 4 and 3(d), Lⁿ(p_α(Q(A))) = Lⁿ(L_{Φ_α(Q)}(A)) = 0 for every α ∈ I(n,P), and Q is a linear isometry of ℝ^P. ∎
proof_key_steps: P < n: there are no multi-indices, and Q = id works.
Replace each piece A ∩ S_j by a Borel hull B_j, which is purely unrectifiable by Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3, and then by a σ-compact C_j ⊆ B_j of full measure.
By bf_projection_null_ae, Lⁿ(L_v(C_j)) = 0 for Lebesgue-a.e. row tuple v ∈ (ℝ^P)^n. The bad set Z is Borel, null and GL(n)-invariant, and Lⁿ(L_v(A)) = 0 for v ∉ Z.
p_α∘Q = L_{Φ_α(Q)}, where Φ_α(Q) is the tuple of rows α of Q.

Haar measure on O(P) (unique right-invariant probability, by a Fubini argument from left invariance) is the law of the row Gram-Schmidt orthonormalization of a Gaussian matrix. For α = (1,…,n) the first n rows are a GL(n)-image of the first n Gaussian rows, so Φ_{α₀}⁻¹(Z) is Haar-null. Permutation matrices and left invariance give the same for every α.
The finite union over α is Haar-null, so a good orthogonal Q exists.

subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, n := m + 1, U ⊆ ℝ^P open, T ∈ D_n(U) with M_W(T) + M_W(∂T) < ∞ for every open W ⊂⊂ U, and μ a Borel measure on ℝ^P with IsMassMeasure T μ such that the upper density Θ*ⁿ(μ, x) (dimensionalUpperDensity μ n univ x) is > 0 for μ-a.e. x. Then there are a Borel set M ⊆ U which is countably n-rectifiable and a Borel function θ : ℝ^P → ℝ with θ > 0 on M and θ Hⁿ-integrable on M ∩ K for every compact K ⊆ U, such that μ = θHⁿ⌞M, i.e. μ = (μHE[n]⌞M).withDensity(x ↦ ofReal θ(x)) (μ(A) = ∫_{A∩M} θ dHⁿ for Borel A).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)), IsOpen U → ∀ T : GeometricCurrentOn U (m + 1), (∀ W, CompactlyContainedOpen W U → T.massOn W + T.boundary.massOn W < ∞) → ∀ μ : Measure (Eucl P), IsMassMeasure T μ → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, 0 < dimensionalUpperDensity μ.toOuterMeasure ((m + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ) univ x) → ∃ (M : Set (Eucl P)) (θ : Eucl P → ℝ), M ⊆ U ∧ MeasurableSet M ∧ CountablyRectifiable (m + 1) M ∧ Measurable θ ∧ (∀ x ∈ M, 0 < θ x) ∧ (∀ K : Set (Eucl P), IsCompact K → K ⊆ U → IntegrableOn θ (M ∩ K) (μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P))) ∧ μ = ((μHE[m + 1] : Measure (Eucl P)).restrict M).withDensity (fun x => ENNReal.ofReal (θ x))
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Ch. 6, proof of Theorem 8.1 (pp. 173-174), displays (1)-(8), in the form of the parent proof's Steps 1-4. Errata/notation: the printed hypothesis Θⁿ(μ_T, x) > 0 is the upper density Θ*ⁿ (as used in (1)-(3)); the ‘Structure Theorem 3.8 of Ch. 3’ of the preamble of §8 is used through Theorem 3.6 and Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3; the measure μ of the hypothesis plays the role of μ_T. The printed proof sets M := {x ∈ U : Θ*ⁿ(μ_T, x) > 0}; here M is first replaced by a Borel set B₀ ⊆ {Θ*ⁿ(μ, ·) > 0} that carries μ, and the Radon-Nikodym theorem is used in its abstract σ-finite form (the form recalled before Simon Ch. 1, 3.24), since Hⁿ⌞B₀ need not be Radon. Hⁿ = μHE[n]; D(x) := Θ*ⁿ(μ, x).

1. Preliminaries. Let W_q (q ∈ ℕ) be open sets ⊂⊂ U with W_q ↑ and ⋃_q W_q = U (exhaustion of the σ-compact open set U; every compact K ⊆ U lies in some W_q). By IsMassMeasure, μ(ℝ^P∖U) = 0 and μ(W_q) = M_{W_q}(T) < ∞; so μ is σ-finite and μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ U. By the sibling mass_measure_abs_continuous, μ ≪ Hⁿ (for all sets).

2. A Borel carrier. The set Z′ := {x : ¬(D(x) > 0)} is μ-null by hypothesis; let Z ⊇ Z′ be a Borel μ-null set (a measurable hull) and B₀ := U∖Z. Then B₀ is Borel, B₀ ⊆ U ∩ {D > 0}, and μ(ℝ^P∖B₀) ≤ μ(ℝ^P∖U) + μ(Z) = 0.

3. σ-finiteness (printed (1)). For j, q ≥ 1 let A_{j,q} := B₀ ∩ W_q ∩ {D ≥ 1/j}. By the sibling density_comparison with V := W_q, A := A_{j,q} and t := 1/j, (1/j) Hⁿ(A_{j,q}) ≤ μ(W_q) < ∞, i.e. Hⁿ(A_{j,q}) ≤ j M_{W_q}(T) < ∞. Every x ∈ B₀ lies in some W_q and has D(x) > 0, hence D(x) ≥ 1/j for some j; so B₀ = ⋃_{j,q} A_{j,q} is a countable union of sets of finite Hⁿ-measure.

4. Rectifiability (printed (6), (7)). By Lemma 3.2 of Ch. 3 in its Borel form (SimonGMT measurable_rectifiable_purelyUnrectifiable_decomposition, applied to the Borel set B₀ and the cover of step 3), B₀ = R ∪ P′ with R Borel and countably n-rectifiable and P′ Hⁿ-measurable and purely n-unrectifiable. Since P′ ⊆ B₀ ⊆ ⋃ A_{j,q}, the sibling structure_projection gives a linear isometry Q with Lⁿ(p_α(Q(P′))) = 0 for all α ∈ I(n,P). As P′ is Hⁿ-measurable, P′ = B ∪ N with B ⊆ P′ Borel and Hⁿ(N) = 0. Then μ(N) = 0 because μ ≪ Hⁿ; and since Lⁿ(p_α(Q(B))) ≤ Lⁿ(p_α(Q(P′))) = 0 for all α, the sibling projection_null gives μ(B) = 0 (this is the use of Remark 2.37(2) in the printed proof). So μ(P′) = 0 (outer measure).

The open set V := O ∩ W_q contains P′ ∩ A_{j,q}, on which D ≥ 1/j, so density_comparison gives (1/j) Hⁿ(P′ ∩ A_{j,q}) ≤ μ(V) < ε. Hence Hⁿ(P′ ∩ A_{j,q}) = 0 for all j, q, and Hⁿ(P′) = 0 because P′ ⊆ ⋃_{j,q} A_{j,q} (printed (6): Hⁿ(P) = 0 for every purely unrectifiable P ⊆ M). Therefore B₀ = R ∪ P′ is countably n-rectifiable (P′ is countably n-rectifiable, being Hⁿ-null, and a union of two countably rectifiable sets is countably rectifiable), and μ = μ⌞B₀ (printed (7)).

5. Radon-Nikodym (printed (8)). Let λ := Hⁿ⌞B₀. λ is σ-finite by step 3 (SimonGMT sigmaFinite_restrict_of_hausdorff_finite_cover), μ is σ-finite (step 1), and μ ≪ λ: if λ(S) = 0 for a Borel S then Hⁿ(S ∩ B₀) = 0, so μ(S ∩ B₀) = 0 (μ ≪ Hⁿ), and μ(S∖B₀) ≤ μ(ℝ^P∖B₀) = 0. By the Radon-Nikodym theorem (Mathlib Measure.withDensity_rnDeriv_eq and Measure.rnDeriv_lt_top) there is a Borel h : ℝ^P → [0, ∞] with μ = λ.withDensity(h), i.e. μ(S) = ∫_{S∩B₀} h dHⁿ for Borel S, and h < ∞ λ-a.e.

6. Positive real density. Let M := B₀ ∩ {0 < h < ∞} (Borel, M ⊆ B₀ ⊆ U, countably n-rectifiable as a subset of B₀) and θ := h.toReal (Borel and real-valued; θ = h ∈ (0, ∞) on M, so θ > 0 on M). For Borel S, μ(S) = ∫_{S∩B₀} h dHⁿ = ∫_{S∩M} h dHⁿ + ∫_{S∩B₀∩{h=0}} h dHⁿ + ∫_{S∩B₀∩{h=∞}} h dHⁿ = ∫_{S∩M} ofReal(θ) dHⁿ, because the second integrand vanishes, the third domain is λ-null, and ofReal(h.toReal) = h on M. Thus μ = (Hⁿ⌞M).withDensity(ofReal ∘ θ).

7. Local integrability. For compact K ⊆ U choose q with K ⊆ W_q; then ∫_{M∩K} θ dHⁿ = μ(M ∩ K) ≤ μ(W_q) = M_{W_q}(T) < ∞, and θ ≥ 0 is Borel, so θ is Hⁿ-integrable on M ∩ K.

8. Summary. M ⊆ U is Borel and countably n-rectifiable, θ is Borel, positive on M and integrable on M ∩ K for every compact K ⊆ U, and μ = θHⁿ⌞M. No dimension assumption is used: if P < n then Hⁿ ≡ 0 on ℝ^P, μ = 0 by μ ≪ Hⁿ, and the argument above applies verbatim (M is then Hⁿ-null and both sides of μ = θHⁿ⌞M vanish). ∎
